# Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the 8 chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> **Tone & Style Directions:** * Voice: First-person, very British, dry, self-deprecating, and anxious. Think *Heartstopper* meets *The End of the F***ing World* meets *Derry Girls* - sincere YA emotion undercut by bleak, absurd humour. Swearing muted to YA level (bloody, piss-taking, twat). * Comedy Source Options: Bathos (huge supernatural dread vs. mundane reality like a leaking ceiling or a BTEC deadline), British Politeness Horror (being too awkward to ask if your friend is actually dying), Class/Gallows Humour (NHS waiting lists, cost of living, grim seaside towns). * Horror Spectrum: Could be fully supernatural (vampires, ritual, folk horror), could be mundane-horror (a nosebleed, a period, a prank gone wrong), or could be ambiguous and stay in the middle (is it real or is it teenage hysteria + group chat paranoia?). * Setting Options: Rain-slicked Northern town (Doncaster, Oldham, Hull, Grimsby), a Welsh valleys comprehensive, a crumbling Cornish seaside town out of season, a dead-end commuter suburb outside London (Croydon, Luton). Sixth-form college as claustrophobic hub. Always cold, always damp, Tesco Meal Deal and Greggs as recurring motifs. The bus never comes. **Character Concepts - Protagonist Options:** * Option A: **Mara Davies, 17.** Year 13, predicted Bs and Cs, works Saturdays at Savers. Anxious, chronically online, the "sensible one" in her friend group who secretly loves true crime podcasts. Narrative voice: frantic, funny, unreliable. * Option B: **Finn Okonkwo, 16.** Year 11, recently moved from London to his mum's tiny hometown in Yorkshire. Outsider, mixed-race, queer, trying painfully hard to fit in. Dry and observant. * Option C: **Jess & Liv (Duo Protagonists).** Sisters, 15 and 17, sharing a bedroom in a council semi. Co-dependent, bickering, code-switching between feral and fiercely loyal. The text interrupts their uneasy truce. **Character Concepts - Sender & Supporting Cast:** * **The Sender Options:** 1. Best friend - e.g., **Priya** - dramatic, attention-seeking, known for cryptic late-night texts after a breakup. Is she in danger or just being Priya? 2. Ex-boyfriend/girlfriend - e.g., **Callum** - who has never used an emoji in his life. Why now? 3. Younger Sibling - e.g., 13-year-old brother **Ellis** who is obsessed with creepypasta and rituals. 4. Mum - who thinks emojis are hieroglyphics and just got a new phone. Accidentally ominous? 5. Unknown Number / Group Chat - No name, just 🩸🩸🩸 from a number everyone thought was disconnected - belongs to someone who left/ghosted/died. 6. The Protagonist Themselves - Sent it while sleep-texting? Pocket dial but with intent? * **The Friend Group:** The sceptic (thinks it's a prank), the believer (into astrology/witchtok), the mum-friend (wants to call an adult immediately). Archetypes to mine for comedy. * **Adult Figures:** Ineffectual but well-meaning - a form tutor who says "have you tried mindfulness?", an NHS 111 operator, a chippy owner who knows everything, a tired single parent working nights. **Plot Interpretations of 🩸🩸🩸:** * **Supernatural / Folk Horror Route:** A dare/ritual. Three drops of blood on a mirror / school bathroom / local landmark (the old mines, the derelict lido, the Wicker Man-adjacent village scarecrow) to summon something. The text is the trigger. "You have to complete it now." Darkly comic because the ancient evil is bureaucratic or pathetic. * **Mundane Misunderstanding Route:** It's not horror at all. It's a period that started at a sleepover, a nosebleed after being punched, a burst spot, ketchup, a prank with fake blood from Halloween that got left in someone's bag. The comedy is the spiralling catastrophising around a totally normal teenage bodily fluid. * **Crime/Thriller Lite Route:** Someone is actually hurt. A fight outside the chicken shop, a house party gone wrong, a self-harm scare. Protagonist has to decide whether to call 999 or if they'll get in trouble for underage drinking. Stakes are real but filtered through teen logistics (how do we get there without waking my dad?). * **Social Horror / Viral Prank Route:** It's a chain message / TikTok trend ("send this to 3 people or you bleed"). Everyone's getting it. Mass hysteria plus British "don't make a fuss" energy. Who started it and why? * **Twisted Comedy Route:** The sender thinks 🩸 is the "tomato" or "rose" emoji. Or it's autocorrect. The dread is entirely in the protagonist's head. **Story Beats & Pacing Ideas for 8 x 1000 Word Chapters (~8000 words total):** * **General Structure to play with:** Three-act structure stretched over 8 chapters. Act I (Ch. 1-2) Setup & Inciting Text, Act II (Ch. 3-6) Escalation & Investigation, Act III (Ch. 7-8) Reveal & Aftermath. Each chapter needs its own mini-arc and cliffhanger to pull reader forward. * **Chapter 1 (~1000w) Beat Options:** Cold open at 00:03. Protagonist is awake revising / doomscrolling / arguing on Discord. Phone lights up: 🩸🩸🩸. Establish voice, setting, immediate relationship to sender. End on unanswered reply: "?? u ok??" left on delivered/read. * **Chapter 2 Beat Options:** The Waiting. Protagonist tries to rationalise, checks sender's socials (last seen, location sharing). Calls - goes to voicemail. Decides to recruit one friend. Worldbuilding: college corridors, the specific grimness of their town. End with discovery that sender was last seen at [local party / woods / abandoned building]. * **Chapter 3 Beat Options:** The Expedition. Protagonist + friend(s) sneak out after midnight. Very British stealth mission (trying not to wake parents, waiting for the 192 night bus that is 40 minutes late). Comic set pieces: climbing a fence in school skirt/trousers, getting chased by someone's tiny yappy dog. * **Chapter 4 Beat Options:** First Twist / False Scare. They find *something* bloody but it's not what they think (a used sanitary pad bin, a dead pigeon, a smashed bottle of Ribena). Tension deflates then re-inflates when they realise sender is NOT there. Phone buzzes again - maybe another 🩸 or a photo. * **Chapter 5 Beat Options:** Midpoint - Lore Dump / Secret Revealed. Flashback to why this ritual/prank/fight matters. Perhaps the friend group has history with this - e.g., they all did the "three drops" game in Year 8, or the sender has been struggling all term and no one noticed properly. Stakes get emotional, not just spooky. * **Chapter 6 Beat Options:** Everything Goes Wrong. Plan falls apart. Adults get involved or almost do. An argument fractures the friend group (you're making this about you / you never take anything seriously). Protagonist is alone. Atmospheric peak - alone in the place where the blood should be. * **Chapter 7 Beat Options:** The Reveal. What 🩸🩸🩸 actually meant. Could play straight horror (something is there), or comic bathos (it was a cry for help about something embarrassingly normal). Subvert expectation - the most effective dark comedy does both: it's funny AND genuinely sad/scary. e.g., Priya did cut herself but it's shallow and she's more embarrassed than dying; or the ritual worked but the demon is just as awkward as they are. * **Chapter 8 Beat Options:** Morning After (~1000w). Daylight makes everything look stupid and less scary. Fallout at school. How the group processes it - memes, apologies, detention. Protagonist reflects on friendship, anxiety, being a teenager where everything feels like life-or-death because it is. Final text callback - protagonist sends 🩸🩸🩸 back as an inside joke / check-in, or deletes the thread. Quiet, bittersweet hopeful ending typical of YA. **Thematic Threads to Sprinkle:** * Anxiety & Catastrophising: The YA brain at 1am makes a single emoji feel like the end of the world. * The Performance of Distress Online: How do you know when a friend is really asking for help vs. posting for effect? * Bodily Horror as Puberty Metaphor: Blood as periods, nosebleeds, shaving cuts, growing up leaking everywhere. * Small-Town Entrapment vs. Loyalty: Wanting to escape but also not wanting to leave your mates behind. # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any specific decisions just yet, just reflecting.> What is landing best here? The strongest tension for Darkly Comic British YA seems to be the gap between *how huge and cinematic the text feels at midnight* and *how relentlessly mundane and awkward the reality of being 17 in Britain is*. If I go full supernatural folk-horror with a legit demon, I risk losing the "British" comedy - it might feel more American YA horror unless the demon is very specifically pathetic, like a local legend about a drowned miner who just wants company or a Tesco-brand vampire. That could be very funny, but I need to be careful it doesn't tip into pure parody and lose genuine YA emotional stakes. If I go purely mundane - like it was just a period or a nosebleed - the comedy is fantastic and very relatable, and it fits YA perfectly, but does three chapters of sneaking around to find out someone started their period feel like enough narrative drive for 8000 words? It works if the *real* story is about friendship and anxiety, with the blood as a MacGuffin, but I’d need to make sure the reader doesn’t feel cheated by the bathos. The dark comedy needs a dark edge: maybe the embarrassment hides something real about self-harm, or shame, or a genuinely bad party situation, so the laugh catches in the throat. The "sender is unknown/ambiguous number" idea is the most classically creepy and gives the best hook for Chapter 1, but YA thrives on known relationships. A text from a BEST FRIEND hits harder emotionally than a text from a spooky unknown. The sweet spot might be a known sender where the *meaning* is unknown. That gives me both dread and character drama. Also, Priya/Callum/Ellis as sender - which one gives the best comedy and allows for an ensemble cast? A best friend gives the most room for guilt/comedy ("I thought you were dying but you just wanted me to bring tampons to the Wetherspoons toilets?"). Pacing-wise, eight chapters at 1000 words is quite tight. I can’t afford a slow burn for four chapters; I need inciting text by page one, and a physical outing by Chapter 3 at the latest or it will feel static. The midnight sneaking-out sequence is probably essential for both comedy and momentum - British YA needs that scene of teenagers trying to be stealthy in puffer jackets while their mum shouts about the heating bill. Chapters 5-6 need to do the heavy lifting: not just more sneaking, but an emotional turn/argument so the middle doesn’t sag into just "looking for blood." Tone is the trickiest balance. "Darkly comic" means the jokes can’t undercut the horror completely - the blood has to matter. If every scary moment is immediately punctured with a joke about Greggs, the dread evaporates. Maybe the model is to let chapters 1-4 be funnier and more frantic, then let chapters 5-7 get quieter and more sincere as the real problem surfaces, then bring the humour back in chapter 8 as coping mechanism. That arc feels very YA - funny kids using humour because they don’t know how to talk about scary stuff. Also thinking about authenticity: the British details will make or break it. It can’t be generic. It needs specifics - the college lanyard, the "on delivered" anxiety, Teams messages from teachers, the weird liminal space of a 24-hour McDonald's after a crisis. If I get that right, even a small story will feel big. What might not work is making the adults too competent - YA needs adults to be peripherally useless or absent at midnight, otherwise why are the kids solving it? But they shouldn’t be caricatures either. So the most compelling version is probably hovering in that middle ground: not full Stephen King, not full pure realism, but a story where teenagers *think* it’s a supernatural ritual because that’s more exciting than admitting their mate is having a mental health wobble or a humiliating normal emergency, and the comedy comes from them preparing for demons when they actually need to bring plasters, a hoodie, and a sincere apology.

Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Synthesised Direction:** The final story will be a Darkly Comic British YA story that lives in the gap between *midnight catastrophising* and *mundane, freezing reality*. It is not full supernatural folk-horror and not a pure bathos prank. The horror is real but human-scale, and the comedy comes from teenagers preparing for a demonic ritual when what they actually need is plasters, a hoodie, and an honest conversation. **Core Choices Made:** * **Plot Interpretation Chosen: Hybrid - The Ritual As Code.** The 🩸🩸🩸 is not a supernatural summoning and not a meaningless typo. It is a revived childhood distress code. In Year 8, the friend group invented "Three Drops" - smear three drops of fake blood / red pen on a bathroom mirror to mean "come get me, no questions, no adults." At 17, Priya uses it for real. The blood is real (a bleeding nose / split lip and cut hand after a messy house party), but not life-threatening. The *dread* is psychological: panic attack, humiliation, and feeling like she can't ask for help properly. This avoids a cheesy literal demon while keeping the folk-horror *feeling* and gives emotional stakes beyond a period joke alone. * **Protagonist & Sender Locked In:** Protagonist is **Mara Davies, 17, Year 13 at Don Valley Sixth Form, Doncaster.** First-person, anxious, dry, self-deprecating, the "sensible one" who secretly loves true crime podcasts and is failing to be sensible. She works Saturdays at Savers. Sender is **Priya Shah, 17, best friend since Year 7** - dramatic, beloved, recently dumped by her college boyfriend, known for cryptic late-night posts. Choosing a best friend over an unknown number maximises YA emotional stakes (guilt, loyalty, irritation) and lets the comedy come from intimacy ("I thought you were being murdered but you're just being Priya again... oh shit, you actually are hurt"). * **Setting Locked In:** Doncaster in late January. Cold, damp, dead. Estate semis, a 24-hour McDonald's, the abandoned Don Valley Lido/Leisure Centre behind college, the unreliable 192 night bus, sixth-form lanyards. Time span: approx 00:03 to 09:00 the next morning - essentially a single night + morning after. * **Voice & Style Intentions:** * **AIM FOR:** First-person past tense with present-tense immediacy, very British, interiority-heavy, conversational. Dry bathos, gallows humour, specificity over stereotype: Tesco Meal Deals, Greggs, NHS 111 hold music, "on delivered" anxiety, Teams messages from tutors, parents shouting about the heating. Humour as a coping mechanism, not a punchline. Dialogue that is funny because it's awkward and polite even in crisis. * **AIM FOR:** A tonal arc. Chapters 1-4 are frantic/funny (catastrophising). Chapters 5-7 get quieter and more sincere as the real vulnerability surfaces. Chapter 8 returns to gentle comedy as repair. The laugh should catch in the throat. * **AVOID:** Full supernatural entity / Americanized horror tropes; making adults competent saviours (they are loving but absent/useless at 1am); making blood/self-harm the joke (dark comedy is about the *reaction*, not the injury); generic Britishness (no "cheerio" or London-only slang); trivialising the distress with a pure period-gag ending where the reader feels cheated. Periods/bodies will be referenced naturally, but not as the sole reveal. * **AVOID:** Glorifying or graphically detailing self-harm. Priya's injuries are accidental/external (punched/nosebleed + cut from broken bottle while drunk/upset) with panic, not intentional self-harm. Keep it YA-appropriate and handle with care. * **Structure & Pacing Intentions (for 8 x ~1000 words = ~8000 words):** * **AIM FOR:** Three-act structure. Act I (Ch 1-2): Inciting text + spiralling wait. Act II (Ch 3-6): Night-time expedition, false scare, lore reveal, and friendship fracture. Act III (Ch 7-8): Real reveal + daylight aftermath/repair. Every chapter will have its own mini-arc and end on a hook/cliffhanger to sustain momentum. No chapter is purely exposition; each moves the physical search forward AND the emotional understanding forward. * **THEMES TO WEAVE:** Anxiety & catastrophising brains at 1am; how teens perform distress online and how hard it is to tell when to take it seriously; bodily autonomy/leakiness as metaphor for growing up; loyalty vs. wanting to escape a small town. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: 00:03 - Delivered** *Word Count Target: ~1000 words. Function: Cold open, voice, inciting incident.* Mara is awake at 00:03 in her box room, revising for mocks, doomscrolling, arguing with her mum about the heating via text. Phone lights up. From Priya: 🩸🩸🩸. No context. Mara's internal spiral begins - Priya never uses the blood emoji, Priya *was* at Jayden's house party tonight. Mara replies "?? priya?? u ok?? love??" - stays on Delivered, then Read with no reply. Checks Priya's Snap Map (last seen 45 mins ago, at the Lido), Insta story (blurry party pic, crying in bathroom). Establishes the friend group dynamic and Mara's anxious voicenarrator. Ends on a second buzz - not a reply, but Priya's live location turns off. **Chapter 2: 00:27 - The Google Search You Don't Want Your Mum To See** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: Escalation in one room, comedy of rationalisation.* Mara tries to be rational and fails. She cycles through theories: ketchup? Period emergency? Chain message? Calls Priya - straight to voicemail with a too-cheerful greeting. She drags in the third friend, **Tyler** (the sceptic, stoned, insists "she's just being dramatic for Jayden"), via group chat. Tyler sends memes, Mara sends a frantic paragraph. She googles "how much blood is dangerous" and "can you die from a nosebleed" while trying not to wake her mum who works early shifts. Discovers Priya and Jayden had a huge public breakup fight at the party via someone's story. Decision point: Mara puts on her massive puffer coat over pyjamas, college lanyard still around neck. Ends as she sneaks out the back door and Tyler reluctantly agrees to meet her at the bus stop - he reveals Priya's last Snap was captioned "three drops lol". **Chapter 3: 01:14 - The Expedition** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: Comic set-piece, physical movement, British stealth mission.* Mara and Tyler's night bus odyssey. The 192 is 37 minutes late, it's pissing it down, Mara forgot gloves. Comedy of trying to be stealthy teenagers in Doncaster (climbing the Lido fence in joggers, Tyler's vape dies, being interrogated by a tiny yappy dog and its owner in a dressing gown). They track Priya's last location to the abandoned Lido toilets behind college - the site of their Year 8 "ritual". Mara explains to reader/Tyler what "Three Drops" meant to them as kids. Tension builds: a light is on in the derelict toilet block. Ends as they push open the graffiti-covered door and see smeared red on the mirror - three distinct drops. **Chapter 4: The Wrong Blood** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: False scare, bathos, re-inflation of stakes.* They find the blood - but it's not Priya. It's a smashed bottle of cherry VK / Ribena and a dead pigeon, or an overflowing sanitary bin that looks horrific under phone torchlight. Tyler: "See? Fucking pigeon. Can we go home?" Deflation and comic relief - Mara feels stupid, angry, cold. Then they realise Priya is NOT there, but her glittery bag is, with her phone inside it (hence no reply) and her coat, and fresh blood on the sink that IS real and still wet. Tyler's phone buzzes - Priya has posted a blurry photo to her Close Friends from *someone else's* phone: the Lido pool itself in the dark, empty, with caption 🩸. They were in the wrong building. Chapter ends as Mara hears a faint crying/retches from the main pool building. **Chapter 5: The Lore Dump** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: Midpoint emotional turn, flashback, raising emotional stakes.* Mara finds Priya huddled by the empty, cracked pool under the emergency light - nose bloody, lip split, hand cut from a broken bottle, mascara everywhere, shivering in a crop top. Not dying, but genuinely hurt and having a panic attack after Jayden humiliated her and she was shoved/ fell. While Tyler runs to the chippy to get help/towels (and fails to get signal), Mara sits with her. Flashback interwoven: Year 8, they invented "Three Drops" after watching a YouTube ritual, using it to get each other out of awkward sleepovers without snitching. Priya whispers: "I didn't know what else to send. Didn't want to bother anyone." The real horror: Priya hasn't been okay for months and Mara was too busy with revision/Savers to notice. Ends with Priya trying to laugh - "Thought you'd think I summoned a demon" - then wincing as her nose bleeds again, more heavily. **Chapter 6: Everything Goes Wrong** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: Lowest point, friendship fracture, isolation.* Attempts to help spiral. Tyler returns with industrial blue paper towels from the chippy and terrible advice. Priya refuses to let them call an adult/ambulance (fear of getting in trouble for drinking, fear of her parents). Mara and Tyler argue fiercely - Tyler says Mara is catastrophising and making it about herself, Mara snaps that Tyler never takes anything seriously. Tyler storms off to "get actual help" leaving Mara alone with Priya. Mara's phone dies. The emergency light flickers out. For a beat, it *is* properly scary and quiet - just two cold, bleeding teenage girls in a massive empty pool, too British to know how to comfort each other properly. Mara realises she has to choose between respecting Priya's "don't tell" and doing the right thing. Ends as Mara makes the decision and runs out into the rain to find Tyler, leaving Priya alone for 30 seconds that feel endless. **Chapter 7: Plasters and Paper Towels** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: Reveal / Rescue / Sincere catharsis.* Mara finds Tyler who *has* called Priya's older sister (19, drives a Corsa, the only competent semi-adult) rather than 999. Together they get Priya out, wrap her hand properly, tilt her forward for nosebleed (Mara recites half-remembered NHS first aid). No demon, no ambulance chase - just competent, unglamorous care. Darkly comic beats (sister says "Jesus wept, Priya, you texted *blood emojis*? I thought you were on your period in Wetherspoons again"). Emotional release: Priya finally sobs properly about Jayden, college pressure, feeling invisible. Mara apologises for being absent. The horror drains, replaced by cold, tired relief. Ends as they sit in the sister's car with heating blasting, Priya's head tipped back with tissue up her nose, Mara holding her cut hand, all of them laughing wetly at how absurd they look. **Chapter 8: Morning After** *Target: ~1000 words. Function: Daylight epilogue, fallout, hopeful repair.* 08:30, Don Valley Sixth Form. Everything looks stupid in daylight. Rumours already flying ("Priya summoned a ghost in the Lido"). Form tutor gives a well-meaning mindfulness worksheet. Mara is exhausted, still in yesterday's clothes, but grounded. Small, quiet scenes: Mara and Priya in the girls' loos, Priya with butterfly plasters on her hand, Mara helping her re-do eyeliner; Tyler buys them all Greggs sausage rolls as apology; Priya's sister has told Priya's mum, who is now fussing in a way that's annoying but loving. Mara reflects in narration on how everything feels like life-or-death at 1am because for teenagers it is. Final beat: That night, Mara texts Priya "u home safe??" Priya replies instantly: 🩸? Mara replies: 🩸🩸🩸 (our code, but now checked, consensual, with a follow-up: "u good? need anything?") - the emoji reclaimed as a genuine check-in, not a panic. Ends on warm, bittersweet, open hopeful note: they are still stuck in Doncaster, but stuck together.

This is a critique & brainstorm only - no rewrite yet. Focused specifically on why this prompt + this plan is vulnerable to LLM defaults. ### 1. How A Human Would Approach This Piece vs. How An LLM Approaches It **A human writing Darkly Comic British YA from `🩸🩸🩸` would likely start from:** * **A specific, lived memory, not a concept.** Not "what could blood mean thematically?" but "that time my mate texted me at 1am from the Wetherspoons toilets and I had to get a taxi I couldn't afford" or "doing a bloody Mary in the school toilets in Year 8 and screaming." The story would be *autobiographically anchored* even if fictionalised. The detail would be weirdly specific and not necessarily plot-useful: the exact way the college lanyard itches, the specific bus stop that always smells of piss, the brand of vape Tyler uses. * **Voice first, plot second.** A human YA writer - especially British - would hear Mara's voice before they know the plot. The comedy would come from a character's *defensive* humour, not jokes inserted to be comic. It would be uneven, sometimes trying too hard, sometimes accidentally cruel. The "dark" would come from intrusive, embarrassing thoughts the narrator is ashamed of having, not from a safely curated "issue." * **An unresolved itch.** Humans are comfortable leaving blood *unexplained or over-explained*. They might never fully clarify if it was a nosebleed + period + cut hand all at once. They might let the reader feel the *annoyance* of being woken up alongside the fear, and let that annoyance linger without resolving it into a lesson. They don't need a thematic reclamation of the emoji in Chapter 8. **An LLM defaults to:** * **Concept first, voice as costume.** It builds a neat thematic engine - "blood = growing up / asking for help" - and then dresses it in a voice that *performs* British YA. It wants to be impressive, coherent, and safe. * **Synthesis and balance.** It wants all interpretations of the prompt to be represented at once - a little folk horror, a little period realism, a little thriller - resulting in the hybrid "ritual as code" compromise. Humans tend to commit to one obsessive, idiosyncratic reading of a prompt. * **Resolution as responsibility.** It feels it must model healthy communication, safe outcomes, and emotional literacy. Humans will let characters be bad friends, say the wrong thing, and not learn a tidy lesson. --- ### 2. Telltale LLM Approaches Generally & Why They Actively Harm *This* Prompt This prompt is kryptonite for LLM defaults because it *requires* being slightly feral, cringe, and unsafe to work. | LLM Telltale | What It Looks Like | Why It Kills This Specific Story | |---|---|---| | **Safety Sanitation** | Injuries are carefully accidental, never self-inflicted. Drinking is present but minimized. No graphic detail. Adults are ultimately benign. Language is "bloody/twat" not actually how teens text. Swearing is asterisked or softened. | Darkly comic YA *needs* to be a bit dangerous. Blood has to be sticky, clotted, embarrassing. If the blood is a sanitized `nosebleed + VK bottle` the audience feels the Author is being careful, not Mara being scared. You can't be "darkly comic" if you're afraid of the dark. The prompt is three blood emojis at midnight - it should feel a little sickening. | | **The Bow-Wrap Ending** | Chapter 8: daylight, Greggs, sister's Corsa, reclaimed emoji as healthy check-in. Everyone learns to communicate. "Stuck together" hopeful closure. | YA is not inherently hopeful in a neat way. A human ending to *this* night would be anti-climactic, slightly sour, administratively annoying. Mum is furious you snuck out. Priya is embarrassed and now ignoring you. The meme goes around school and you hate it. LLMs wrap with a bow because they are trained to be satisfying and therapeutic. This story needs to end with a frayed thread, not a bow. | | **Impressive Writing Over Readable Voice** | Lyrical introspection, perfect metaphors for anxiety, poetic three-beat lists: "cold, damp, dead." Sentences with elegant em-dash asides and balanced clauses. "The dread is psychological" type thesis statements. | A 17-year-old Doncaster girl at 1am does not think in polished literary metaphors. Her internal monologue is repetitive, catastrophising, typo-ridden, referencing TikTok audio. LLM "beautiful writing" flattens character voice into one generic sensitive-narrator voice. The comedy dies when every line is trying to be quotable. | | **The Explainy Spoon-Feed** | Characters articulate theme for the reader: "I didn't know what else to send. Didn't want to bother anyone." / "everything feels like life-or-death because for teenagers it is." Lore is delivered in a clean flashback exposition dump. | Real teens are inarticulate when bleeding and panicking. They mumble, deflect with jokes, say "dunno" and "it's not even that deep." LLMs over-explain because they fear the reader won't get it. For this story, the horror *is* the failure to articulate. The plan's Chapter 5 "Lore Dump" is a classic LLM tell - humans would leak lore messily, in fragments, possibly misremembered. | | **Curated Quirk / Checklist Britishness** | Greggs, Tesco Meal Deal, NHS 111, Wetherspoons, "puffer coat," "lanyard," Doncaster as a name-drop, chippy, Cuppa - all correct but selected like a mood board for an American reader. Diversity as checklist: Mara Davies, Priya Shah, Tyler - ethnically diverse, politically frictionless. | Real British specificity is more boring and more weird: the specific Year 13 common room with the broken microwave that trips the electrics, the UCAS deadline you missed, the BTEC vs A-Level divide, the actual bus number with the actual delay pattern, the specific slang for that town. LLM Britishness feels like tourism. It also avoids class friction - a Savers job is mentioned but never *felt* as shame/money stress. | | **Symmetrical, Even Pacing & Perfect Structure** | 8 chapters x 1000 words, each with a clear function, cliffhanger, escalation. Three-act structure textbook perfect. | A human's 8 chapters would be uneven. Chapter 3 might be 600 words of just waiting for the bus. Chapter 6 might be 1,400 words of a single argument that goes in circles. The LLM's perfect architecture makes the night feel *designed*, not *experienced*. Midnight dread is not symmetrical. | | **Likeable, Self-Aware Protagonist** | Mara is anxious but endearing, self-deprecating in a charming way, loves true crime podcasts, "the sensible one." She is always ultimately kind and introspective. | A human Mara would be less likeable at 1am. She would be resentful: "Why is Priya doing this *again*?" She would have a flicker of "if she's dead I'll be annoyed I have to do her coursework." She would be a bit of a dick to Tyler. LLMs sand off unlikeability because they are trained to be likeable. Dark comedy *needs* that flash of selfishness. | | **Therapy-Speak & Moralising** | Focus on "emotional stakes," "healthy communication," "processing," "boundaries," "asking for help." The story becomes a lesson about mental health literacy. | Teens don't think in therapy-speak while sitting in an abandoned lido. They think "oh god, is this my fault? will she be sick on me?" The LLM turns a visceral night into a PSA. It's safe, but it's not funny or dark. It makes the story *about* a theme rather than *through* character. | --- ### 3. Deep Dive Critique: How The Current Intention & Plan Is Already Falling Into LLM Traps The plan is competent, well-paced, and emotionally responsible - which is exactly the problem. It is *too* responsible to be human. **A. The Core Concept is a Classic LLM Compromise:** > "Hybrid - The Ritual As Code... not supernatural, not meaningless typo... a revived childhood distress code." This is the LLM desire for synthesis and safety. It wants to honour *all* brainstorm ideas at once and offend none. It's clever, neat, and symbolically tidy. A human would more likely pick a *messier, dumber* interpretation and commit: e.g., Priya *did* think she was summoning something because she was off her head, or it *was* just her period and she was too embarrassed to say, and Mara overreacted massively. The "code" idea is touching, but it's also *too* screenwriterly-perfect. It gives the blood a *meaningful, wholesome origin story* which defangs it. Real codes between friends are never that elegantly reclaimed - they're cringe, half-forgotten, and someone always misremembers them. **B. Sanitised Stakes via Safety Bias:** > "Priya's injuries are accidental/external (punched/nosebleed + cut from broken bottle while drunk/upset) with panic, not intentional self-harm. Keep it YA-appropriate and handle with care." This sentence *is* the LLM tell. The plan is actively working to make the blood *not too dark* to avoid triggering the safety filter. But the prompt is `🩸🩸🩸` - if you defang it this much, the "dark" in darkly comic vanishes. The plan ensures no one is really responsible (she was "shoved/fell"), no one is really in danger ("not life-threatening"), and the resolution requires no system (no A&E, no police). A human writer would sit more uncomfortably in the ambiguity: did Jayden push her? Did she cut her hand on purpose or by accident while drunk? Is this the first time? The plan's careful wording guarantees a comfortable, non-graphic, non-blameworthy incident. It feels managed. **C. The Deus Ex Corsa (Chapter 7):** > "Tyler *has* called Priya's older sister (19, drives a Corsa, the only competent semi-adult)" LLMs love a mildly competent older sister / cool young adult who can solve the problem without invoking scary institutions like the NHS or police. It's a *safe* rescue - intimate, low-consequence, comedic. It avoids the more human, more awkward outcomes: actually having to call 111 and being on hold for 45 minutes; a paramedic being brusque; Priya's mum actually being woken up and being *angry* rather than fussing lovingly; Tyler actually *not* calling anyone because he's scared. The sister is a narrative safety net that lets the story stay cosy. **D. The Thematically Perfect Ending:** > "Final beat: ...Mara texts Priya 'u home safe??' Priya replies: 🩸? Mara replies: 🩸🩸🩸 (our code, but now checked, consensual)... the emoji reclaimed as a genuine check-in" This is textbook LLM bow-wrap. It's a symmetrical callback that turns a distress signal into a healed, healthy communication tool. It's satisfying, symbolic, and completely *unlike* how teens actually text after a crisis. A human ending would be more anticlimactic, asymmetrical, or even slightly sour: Mara sends a meme, Priya leaves her on read for a day, they never talk about the blood again and it becomes an in-joke that is also a scab. The reclaimed emoji is *too* healed. It tells the reader "the lesson was learned." **E. Voice & Comedy Pitfalls:** The plan *describes* the voice as "dry, self-deprecating, anxious, conversational" but then plans jokes that are *LLM British Comedy Greatest Hits*: mindfulness worksheet, Greggs sausage rolls, tiny yappy dog in dressing gown, vape dies, blue paper towels from chippy. These are not *wrong*, but they are *expected*. They are the jokes an LLM has seen work for "Britishness" a thousand times. A human's dark comedy here would be more specific and more uncomfortable: e.g., Mara worrying about her mum seeing the Savers uniform is bloody, or calculating the Uber cost home, or Priya apologising for bleeding on Mara's *new* puffer, or finding the blood is mixed with fake tan streaks. The plan's humour is *observational* (look at Britain!) not *characterological* (look at my shame!). **F. Structural Over-Neatness:** Every chapter has a labelled function: Inciting incident, False scare, Lore dump, Lowest point, Rescue. The "false scare = pigeon/VK" is a classic LLM fake-out that is signposted as a fake-out. The pacing is TV-episode perfect. A human's short story over 8 chapters would likely have a saggy middle, a chapter that is just waiting, a reveal that comes too early and then has to be sat with. The plan's desire to make *every* chapter move both plot and emotional understanding forward is efficient but inhumanly tidy. **G. Articulate Trauma:** > "Priya hasn't been okay for months and Mara was too busy with revision/Savers to notice." This is an adult, retrospective understanding. At 1am in a freezing pool, a real Priya wouldn't deliver this clean summary. She'd say "You never text anymore anyway" or she'd deflect. The plan makes characters *understand themselves* in real time to ensure the theme is clear. That is the LLM's didactic impulse. --- ### 4. Brainstorm: Ideas To Make It More Human, Less LLM Not a rewrite, just raw material to pull from to inject friction, specificity, and imperfection: **Make Mara Less Likeable / More Human:** * Let her first thought after `🩸🩸🩸` be irritation, not just fear: "For fuck's sake, Priya, I'm literally failing Chemistry." Let her consider *not* going. * Give her a petty, shameful intrusive thought she never voices: *if Priya is actually hurt, do I get to miss mocks?* Then let her hate herself for thinking it. * Make her an unreliable narrator about the friendship: she insists they are best friends, but small details betray distance - she doesn't know Priya's new boyfriend's surname, she misremembers the "Three Drops" rules. * Let her be a bad comforter: she tries to use a true-crime podcast line to soothe Priya and it lands horribly. She laughs at the wrong moment. **Make The Blood Messier & Less Symbolic:** * Don't let it be *just* nosebleed + cut hand. Make it unglamorous: period blood leaked through onto the back of her skirt + a nosebleed + fake tan + glitter, so Mara can't tell what is what and is too embarrassed to ask. The comedy/horror is *not knowing* where blood is coming from. * Or let the amount be ambiguous: is that a lot of blood or does it just *look* like a lot because it's smeared with water on white tiles? Mara's googling is useless because she can't estimate. * Keep one detail unexplained: Whose blood is on the *second* sink? Do we ever find out? Maybe not. * Avoid making it "still wet and fresh" - that's thriller shorthand. Maybe it's already drying and flaking, which is more disconcerting. **Make Britishness Lived, Not Curated:** * Replace generic Greggs with *specific* Greggs order that signals character: Tyler always gets a steak bake even though it burns his mouth, Mara gets the cold vegan sausage roll because it's 80p cheaper. * Money as a real texture: Mara can't afford a taxi, her phone is on 8% and she has no data, the night bus costs £3.80 she doesn't have in cash. She screenshots her mum's bank warning text. * College specifics: Not just "lanyard," but the lanyard that snaps, the BTEC Health & Social vs A-Level divide, the Teams message from Miss that says "Mara, you missed intervention" at 07:00. * Language: Less "bloody hell," more actual Doncaster teen texting: "hahahaha no but fr r u ok", "pls dont be dead lol", dropped capitals, voice notes that are 3 seconds long. Priya's `🩸🩸🩸` is *more* chilling because she *never* uses emojis properly - she types "hahahahah" not "😂". **Make The Structure Lopsided:** * Let Chapter 2 be *too long* - just Mara in bed spiralling, refreshing Priya's location, arguing with Tyler who keeps sending TikToks, eating dry cereal. Nothing happens and that's the point. Anxiety is boring. * Let the "Lore Dump" not be a dump. Priya remembers the game wrong. Mara remembers it as three drops on the *mirror*, Priya remembers it as three drops on *paper*. That small mismatch hurts more than perfect recall. * Delay the find: Make them search the *wrong* place for a whole chapter and be cold and bickering the entire time. Let Tyler actually go home at one point and leave Mara alone. **Make The Dark Darker, The Comic More Uncomfortable:** * Humour that *fails* to be funny: Mara makes a joke about the lido being haunted and Priya starts crying harder. Tyler does a bit that no one laughs at and it hangs in the air. * Dark without being heavy: Priya says "I just didn't want to go home like this, my mum would kill me" - the dark is parental shame, reputation, not just physical danger. Or she was trying to avoid being seen drunk because her mum thinks she's at revision. * Let the adults be *worse* than benign: Mum is not fussing lovingly, she's exhausted and says "Priya, you can't keep doing this to Mara." The sister is hungover and annoyed she had to drive. The chippy guy doesn't help, he tells them to piss off. **Break The Therapeutic Resolution:** * No reclaimed emoji. Maybe Mara deletes the `🩸🩸🩸` thread because she can't look at it. Or she mutes Priya for a day because she's angry and then feels guilty. * Don't let them have a big cathartic talk by the pool. Let Priya say "Can we not do this here?" and they sit in silence until the sister comes. The real talk happens three days later via awkward voice notes, not in the cinematic pool. * Leave a social cost: Someone filmed Priya crying in the pool and it's on someone's story by morning. They have to deal with *that*, not just their feelings. The night doesn't stay private. * End with Mara still unsure if she did the right thing. Did she overreact? Underreact? She checks Priya's location one last time even though she knows it's fine. The anxiety doesn't resolve with a lesson. * Let the last line be bathetic, not poetic. Not "stuck together," but something petty and true: "My puffer still smelled of the pool for a week." **Add Sensory & Fragmentary Human Texture:** * First-person tics: Mara repeating phrases, correcting herself mid-sentence, leaving a sentence unfinished because she's cold. * Specific physical feeling: Blood under fingernails that won't wash off, the way a nosebleed tastes like battery acid, the way cheap toilet paper disintegrates when wet. * Make time drag: Note the actual timestamps as headers but have Mara lose track. "My phone said 01:14. Then it said 01:15. Then it said 01:15 again for ages." This is all about trading the LLM's neat, kind, impressive, explainy story for one that is a bit more selfish, inconsistent, cringe, and lingering - which is what makes darkly comic British YA feel like it was lived, not generated.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core Premise Synthesised:** This is a Darkly Comic British YA story about a text that feels like a horror movie at midnight and turns out to be a humiliating, cold, human mess by morning. The comedy is defensive and often fails; the dark is not a demon but shame, money, and being too awkward to ask for help properly. **Plot Choice - Committed & Messy, Not Hybrid-Safe:** The `🩸🩸🩸` is Priya re-using a half-remembered Year 8 game called "Three Drops" - but she remembers it wrong, Mara remembers it wrong, and neither is sure if it's still a real code. This is not a neat, wholesome reclaimed symbol. It's a cringe kids' ritual (mirror / pen / TikTok witchcraft) dragged into a real night where it doesn't fit. The blood itself is deliberately unglamorous and un-diagnosable in the moment: a nosebleed from being shoved/falling at Jayden's party + a cut palm from a broken VK bottle + period blood leaked through - mixed with water, fake tan and glitter so Mara can't tell what she's looking at. It looks like a lot because it's smeared on white tiles. It is not life-threatening, which is exactly why Mara feels guilty for being so scared and so *annoyed* at the same time. No supernatural entity. No single clean explanation. The question "is this a lot of blood?" is never cleanly answered, which is truer to a 17-year-old googling at 1am. I am intentionally avoiding the LLM compromise of a perfect hybrid. I am committing to the *dumb, embarrassing* reading: two teenagers who prepared for a ritual/murder and actually needed to deal with a bleeding, drunk, freezing mate who doesn't want her mum to see her like this. **Voice & Style - Character First, Not Impressive:** * **AIM FOR:** First-person, close, inconsistent Mara Davies (17, Year 13, Don Valley Sixth Form, Doncaster, Savers on Saturdays). Her narration is repetitive, petty, and intrusive. She corrects herself mid-sentence, repeats phrases when anxious, leaves thoughts unfinished. Sentences fragment when she's cold. Present-tense immediacy inside past-tense narration. She is not charmingly self-deprecating; she is sometimes a bad friend - resentful, calculating the cost of a taxi, thinking *if she's actually hurt do I get out of mocks?* and hating herself for it. * **AIM FOR:** Humour as failed coping, not quips. Jokes that land badly, hang in the air, or are immediately regretted. Bathos that is embarrassing, not cute. Britishness via *lived* boredom, not a checklist: the specific broken microwave in the common room, the BTEC/A-Level divide, UCAS emails at 7am, the 192 that is always 37 minutes late, the £3.80 bus fare she doesn't have, phone on 8% with no data, the lanyard that actually snaps. * **AVOID:** Lyrical, essayistic "anxiety is..." metaphors, balanced three-beat literary lists, thesis statements about being a teenager. Avoid therapy-speak ("boundaries", "processing", "holding space"). Characters will be inarticulate under stress - they say "dunno", "it's not even that deep", deflect with "hahahaha". No clean lore dump; information leaks in fragments and contradictions. * **AVOID:** Sanitised language. Texts will be in lower-case, typo-ridden, with 3-second voice notes. Swearing is casual and low-level (pissed, twat) but not asterisked. Blood will be tactile and gross (metallic taste, clotted, toilet paper disintegrating, blood under nails) without being graphic or glorifying self-harm. The injury is accidental and alcohol-adjacent, not intentional self-harm. **Structure & Pacing - Deliberately Lopsided for 8 x 1000 Words:** * **AIM FOR:** A night that *feels* like a night - boring, stretched, then suddenly too fast. I will not make 8 perfectly symmetrical episodes with identical arcs. Some chapters will be intentionally slow/boring (anxiety is boring), some will be cramped. The search will go to the *wrong* place for too long. The "reveal" will come slightly too early and then we have to sit in the awkward aftermath, which is the actual story. * **AIM FOR:** Serving the prompt throughout. `🩸🩸🩸` is not just the hook. It is re-seen, misread, and stressed over in every chapter - on delivered, on read, no reply, location off, Close Friends post. The final chapter will not reclaim it as a healed symbol. * **AVOID:** The LLM safety net and bow-wrap. No competent older sister who solves everything kindly. No Greggs-as-group-hug, no reclaimed emoji as healthy check-in, no "stuck together" poetic closure. The rescue will be bureaucratic, annoying, and inadequately adult. The ending will be sour, gossipy, and unresolved - the night becomes a story at school that Priya hates, Mara is still checking locations, and Mara's puffer smells of chlorine for a week. **What This Story Is *About* Without Saying It:** Class and money as texture (can't afford to help properly), the performance of distress online and the panic of not knowing when to take it seriously, and how friendship at 17 is loyalty mixed with resentment. The dark comedy comes from the gap between cinematic dread and having to ask a chippy guy for help while bleeding. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: 00:03 - Delivered [~1000w]** Function: Irritation before fear. Establish unlikeable, human Mara. Mara is awake revising, phone on 8%, mum asleep before early shift. `🩸🩸🩸` from Priya. First thought is *annoyance*, not terror - Priya does this for attention after Jayden, Mara has mocks. She replies "priya?? u ok??" - Delivered. Then Read. No reply. She checks Snap Map (Priya at Jayden's, last seen 43m ago), finds a blurry Close Friends story of Priya crying in a bathroom. Her spiralling is petty and intrusive: calculates Uber cost, thinks about missing mocks, refreshes location obsessively. Time drags - 00:03 to 00:04 feels like an hour. End hook: Priya's live location turns off mid-refresh, not with a dramatic ping but just gone. **Chapter 2: 00:27 - The Boring Spiral [~1000w]** Function: Anti-climax. Anxiety as boring, static waiting. Lopsided by design. Nothing happens and that's the point. Mara is still in bed, getting colder, arguing with Tyler on chat who keeps sending TikToks and saying "she's just dramatic lol". She calls Priya - straight to too-cheerful voicemail. She googles "how much blood is bad nosebleed" and gets useless NHS fluff. She drags Tyler into coming not because he's noble but because she bribes/guilt-trips him. Money texture: no cash for bus, has to steal £5 from her own tips. She puts puffer over pyjamas, college lanyard still on. She sneaks out via back door and hears mum cough. The "Three Drops" is mentioned for the first time but misremembered - Mara thinks mirror, Tyler thinks paper. End hook: Tyler finally says "wait she posted 'three drops lol' on private story 1hr ago" - too late, Mara is already outside in the rain. **Chapter 3: 01:14 - The Wrong Building [~1000w]** Function: Comic set-piece where comedy fails. Mara + Tyler wait for the 192 which is 37 mins late, pissing it down, vape dead, both furious and performing being fine. They walk instead, bickering about who is a better friend. They go to the abandoned Lido toilet block behind college because that's where they *think* the game was. They find red smears - three drops - on the mirror. Beat of real dread. Then torch reveals it's cherry VK + a pigeon, and a sanitary bin that looks like a horror set under phone light. Tyler is vindicated and wants to go home; Mara feels stupid and suddenly angry at Priya. Then they find Priya's glitter bag, coat, and phone *with no Priya* - and a wet sink with diluted real blood that is not VK. Their phones buzz - a new Close Friends photo from *someone else's phone*: the empty Lido pool in the dark. They were in the wrong building. End hook: faint crying/retching from the main pool shed, barely audible over rain. **Chapter 4: The Wrong Kind of Blood [~1000w]** Function: Bathos sustained. The blood is unreadable. They find Priya by the cracked, empty pool. She's shivering in a crop top, nose bleeding, lip split, palm cut, tights laddered, fake tan streaked, glitter + blood smeared together. Mara cannot tell what blood is what - nose? hand? period? She is too embarrassed to ask and too scared to look. Attempts at first aid are incompetent: blue chippy paper towels that disintegrate, tilting head back wrong, Tyler offering a vape. Priya is not dying but is having a panic attack and is mortified about being seen. No big speech. Tyler goes to find signal/help, leaving Mara alone. The two girls sit in awkward silence; Mara makes a true-crime joke that dies horribly. End hook: Priya whispers "Don't tell anyone, please, my mum thinks I'm at revision" and her nose starts bleeding heavily again. **Chapter 5: We Did It Wrong [~1000w]** Function: Fragmented lore, not a dump. Emotional stakes without articulacy. While waiting, Priya and Mara try to talk and fail. The "Three Drops" memory comes out in contradictory scraps - Priya thought it was three drops of blood on paper to summon something, Mara thought it was red pen on mirror to mean "come get me no adults." Neither is sure. Flashback is not narrated cleanly but as bickering corrections. Priya reveals in stops and starts: Jayden shouted at her, someone shoved her, she fell into the bottles, she ran to the Lido because it was close and she didn't want to go home drunk/bleeding. She says "I didn't know what else to send that you'd actually come" then immediately deflects with "it's not even that deep lol sorry". Mara realises they've barely texted properly in weeks but doesn't say it well. End hook: Tyler returns, not with help but having achieved nothing - chippy guy told him to piss off, no signal, sister not answering. **Chapter 6: Leave Her Alone For 30 Seconds [~1000w]** Function: Fracture. Lowest point is interpersonal, not supernatural. Full argument. Mara wants to call Priya's older sister/mum; Priya begs not to. Tyler snaps that Mara is catastrophising and making it about herself; Mara snaps that Tyler never takes anything seriously. Tyler actually *leaves* to go get the sister by walking to her flat, leaving Mara and Priya alone. Mara's phone dies. Emergency light flickers out. For ~200 words it's properly scary and quiet - just breathing, rain, blood taste, the huge empty pool. Mara has to decide without a big monologue. She stays, holds pressure on Priya's hand with her own scarf, which will be ruined. End hook: Mara decides to break Priya's confidence and runs out into the rain after Tyler, leaving Priya alone for what feels like forever, hating herself. **Chapter 7: Paper Towels, Not Plasters [~1000w]** Function: Bad rescue. Competence is annoying and unglamorous. No hero moment. Tyler has got Priya's 19-year-old sister, Chloe, who is hungover, in pyjamas, driving a Corsa with a cracked windshield and is *annoyed*, not maternal. She is brisk, slightly shaming: "Jesus, Priya, blood emojis? I thought you were taking the piss." She does basic first aid correctly (lean forward, pinch, pressure with actual gauze from the car), which makes Mara feel incompetent. They don't call 999; Chloe drives them to urgent care's waiting room where they sit for ages and then leave because Priya refuses to go in. Dark comedy is administrative: forms, parking, Chloe arguing with Priya's mum on speaker. No cathartic pool-side confession - Priya asks "can we not do this here?" and they sit in heated car in silence, Priya with tissue up nose, Mara holding her bloody scarf. End hook: Chloe says "You're telling Mum you fell, yeah? And you're paying to get this car valeted." **Chapter 8: 08:30 - Common Room [~1000w]** Function: Sour daylight aftermath. No bow. Morning at Don Valley. Everything looks stupid. Rumour already spreads - someone filmed Priya at the Lido and it's on a private story captioned "lido ritual gone wrong lmao". Priya is mortified and is now giving Mara the cold shoulder for telling Chloe. Form tutor hands Mara a mindfulness worksheet and asks if she's okay in front of everyone. Mara is exhausted, still in yesterday's joggers, common room microwave trips the electrics again. Money/shame texture: Mara has to explain the ruined scarf to her mum, who is tired and says "you can't keep doing this for Priya, love". Small repair is not symbolic: Tyler buys too-hot steak bakes, Priya lets Mara fix her eyeliner in the toilets but doesn't really talk. Final beat is intentionally anticlimactic: Mara goes home, her puffer still smells of chlorine and wet concrete. She looks at the `🩸🩸🩸` thread, doesn't reclaim it, just deletes the notification and then mutes Priya for the night because she's still angry, then un-mutes her and checks her location one last time. Last line is bathetic and true, not poetic: "It was 8 quid in the wash to get the blood out and it still didn't come out properly."

# Mara Davies **Background, Personality, Idiosyncrasies, Flaws:** 17, Year 13 at Don Valley Sixth Form. Does BTEC Health & Social plus A-Level Psychology (retaking one paper) because she was told she wasn't "academic enough" for three A-Levels and has never forgiven anyone for it. Works Saturdays and Wednesdays after college at Savers on Frenchgate for £6.80 an hour. Lives with her mum (Lisa, 43, domiciliary carer) in a semi on the Balby estate - dad hasn't been in the picture since she was 9, texts at Christmas. Mara is the anxious "sensible one" who is desperate to stop being the sensible one. She is a catastrophic overthinker who masks it as being organised. She has 14 unsent drafts in her notes app, all starting "sorry if this is weird but...". She is a people-pleaser who keeps score. She will say "no worries!!" then be furious about it for three days and not say why. Core flaw is resentful loyalty. She *wants* to be needed - being needed by Priya is her identity - but she deeply resents the cost. When Priya texted `🩸🩸🩸` her first feeling isn't pure fear, it's a flash of *are you fucking kidding me, I have mocks* followed immediately by shame for thinking it. She has intrusive, transactional thoughts she hates: *if Priya's actually in hospital do I get extenuating circumstances?* She holds petty grudges and revises history to make herself the more neglected friend. Trivial anchors: She bites the skin around her nails until they bleed, then picks Savers hand cream (the cheap coconut one) compulsively. Always cold. Has one puffer coat that is too big and smells faintly of the Savers stockroom. Chews the inside of her cheek when revising. Phone is always on 8% because she never charges it overnight in case of fire. Keeps her college lanyard on at home without noticing. Listens to true crime podcasts at 1.5x speed to feel competent about danger. Collects screenshots of Priya's stories but never confronts her. Her revision notes are colour-coded then immediately abandoned. **Physicality:** 5'4, pale in a way that never tans, just goes pink and peels. Long dark hair she scrapes into a low ponytail because she can't be bothered. Cracked lips, chapped hands from work. Wears the same black joggers three days running, puffer zipped to chin even indoors. Carries herself small - shoulders up, arms crossed, takes up no space. Walks fast, head down, like she's trying to get somewhere before anyone talks to her. When anxious she goes completely still and goes quiet, which people read as calm. It's not. She smiles with her mouth closed. When she cries her nose streams, not cute. **Motives, Allegiances, Relationships:** Motivation is to get out - she has a conditional offer for Adult Nursing at Sheffield Hallam that she is terrified of losing and terrified of getting. She wants to be seen as capable, not "sweet". Allegiance is to Priya first, even over herself, but it's fraying. She feels Tyler doesn't try hard enough and is jealous that he can opt out. She is loyal to her mum in a practical way (does washing, cooks tea) but hides things because she doesn't want to be another job for her mum. To Priya: Thinks "we're best friends since Year 7" but can't remember the last time they hung out without a crisis. Keeps a mental ledger of who texted last. To Tyler: Affectionate contempt. She relies on him to be the sceptic so she can be the worrier. Secretly thinks he's a bit of a waster but would be gutted if he left the group chat. To herself: Wants to be a good person, is scared she's actually quite selfish. **Voice:** > *Internal, 00:04:* `read at 00:04. ok. ok so she's read it. so she's got her phone. so she's choosing not to reply. unless she's dead. oh my god. don't be dramatic. she does this. she LOVES doing this. i should just go to sleep. i can't go to sleep now.` > *Dialogue, trying to comfort:* "Do you want... like... do you want me to - I read that you're supposed to pinch it but not tilt back, or - sorry, I'm doing this wrong, I'm so sorry -" # Priya Shah **Background, Personality, Idiosyncrasies, Flaws:** 17, Year 13, same form as Mara. British Indian, lives with parents and younger brother in a new-build in Bessacarr - a bit more money than Mara's family, which neither of them ever mentions but both feel. Parents run a pharmacy, very present, very high-expectation, very "we don't talk about feelings we talk about grades." She is predicted AAB and crumbling under it. Priya is dramatic, lovable, and exhausting on purpose. She performs distress beautifully - the blurry bathroom selfie, the cryptic story, the 2am voice note - because performance is the only way she's learned to be noticed without being told off for being needy. She is funny, warm, extremely loyal when she's not spiralling, but she lies constantly about small things to avoid conflict. "I'm at Mia's revising" = I'm at Jayden's. "My period's just heavy" = I don't want to explain. Core flaw is avoidance through performance. She would rather send three emojis than type "I'm drunk and bleeding and I don't want my mum to see me." She tests friendships to see who will come without being asked directly, then is devastated when people get it wrong. She rewrites events immediately after they happen to make them funnier/less embarrassing. Deeply ashamed of being seen as messy. Trivial anchors: Always glittery - glitter eyeshadow that migrates everywhere, gets in Mara's puffer and never leaves. Fake tan that goes patchy on her ankles. Cropped tops even in January, then complains she's cold as a personality trait. Types "hahahahaha" instead of using laughing emojis, but uses 🩸 dead seriously. Leaves voice notes that are 17 seconds of "sorry sorry sorry wait - " then silence. Has Priya's mum's pharmacy plasters in her bag but never uses them. Vapes cherry ice and denies it to her parents. Never deletes photos, has 19,000 in camera roll. **Physicality:** 5'2, pretty in a way that's very effortful - full brows she tints herself, long black hair straightened to death, acrylics she picks off. Wears small gold hoops, even to bed. Carries herself big when confident (takes up space, loud laugh) and completely folded in when embarrassed (knees to chest, hair curtain, won't make eye contact). When drunk/upset her eyeliner transfers to everywhere. Her hands shake when she's panicking and she hides it by holding her sleeves. Bleeds a lot and acts like it's nothing, which is scarier than if she made a fuss. **Motives, Allegiances, Relationships:** Motive is to be held without having to ask to be held. Wants to be seen as okay and fun, not as "the one who needs checking on." Wants to stay in Doncaster near family vs. Mara wanting to leave, and feels Mara pulling away. To Mara: "My person" - but she knows Mara is tired of her. Sends `🩸🩸🩸` specifically because Mara is the only one who would remember Year 8 Three Drops, even if half-remembered. That's trust, weaponised. To Jayden (ex, 18, works at McDonald's, college leaver): Still wants him to care, hates him. The party shove/fall happens because she went to prove she was fine. To Parents/Chloe (older sister, 19): Loves them, performs "good daughter" for them, terrified of being a disappointment. Chloe is the only adult she'll accept help from because Chloe won't lecture. **Voice:** > *Text, unsent draft she actually sent:* `🩸🩸🩸` `sorry` > *Dialogue, shivering by the pool, deflecting:* "Don't look, it's gross - it's not even that much, it's just - I've got tan on, it makes it look - hahaha, do you remember when we thought we actually summoned that woman in the toilets? God, we're so thick." # Tyler Bennett **Background, Personality, Idiosyncrasies, Flaws:** 17, Year 13, joined Don Valley in Year 10 from an academy in Scunny after his parents split. Lives with his dad who works nights at the warehouse, so Tyler basically lives alone with a PS4 and a chest freezer full of pizza. Does BTEC Sport, told everyone he's going to be a personal trainer, has no plan. The classic "can't be arsed" boy who is actually quite anxious and uses not caring as armour. Tyler is the group sceptic, not because he's wise but because caring is cringe. His default is deflection - meme, joke, vape trick. He is lazy, reliably 20 minutes late, loses everything, but he *does* show up if guilt-tripped enough, which he resents. He deals with blood/feelings by making it about logistics: "how much is a taxi", "my dad's gonna kill me if I'm out". Core flaw is avoidant loyalty. He wants to be liked for being chill, so he minimises everything. He will say "she's just being dramatic for Jayden lol" because it's easier than considering Priya is actually hurt. When he realises he was wrong, he overcorrects with frantic, useless action (running to the chippy for paper towels instead of calling anyone). Terrified of being seen as soft, so he is cruel in tiny ways without meaning to be. Trivial anchors: Always in the same Nike joggers with a hole in the pocket where his vape falls through. Vape is almost always dead, he charges it with a frayed cable. Says "safe" and "innit" constantly. Sends TikToks instead of replies. Has a chipped front tooth from Year 9 he never fixed. Keeps his dad's blue paper towels from work in his bag because he gets nosebleeds too. Eats while other people are crying and doesn't notice. Bad at eye contact when it's serious, looks at floor. **Physicality:** Tall, lanky, 6'0 but slouches to 5'10. Hood up even indoors. Hands in sleeves, weight on one leg. Moves slow until he has to move fast, then clumsy - trips over the Lido fence, smacks his shin and says "I'm fine" while limping. When scared his voice goes higher and he laughs too much. Carries himself like he's trying to take up negative space - makes himself smaller by being vague. **Motives, Allegiances, Relationships:** Motive is to keep everything low-stakes. Doesn't want to be responsible for anyone's big feelings because he doesn't know what to do with his own. Allegiance is to the group chat as an institution - he doesn't want the group to split because then he'd have to choose. To Mara: Thinks she's a stress-head but respects that she actually does things. Lets her be the responsible one so he doesn't have to be. Feels guilty she does more for Priya than he does. To Priya: Fancies her a bit, would never say, so he is extra dismissive to cover it. Feels extra guilty when she's actually hurt. To Dad/Sister etc: No real adult backup, so he invented Chloe as a solution - calling Priya's sister is his version of calling an adult without calling *his* adult. **Voice:** > *Group chat, 00:31:* `mara bffr she's jus tryna make jayden jel lol` `she did this last time after oceana` `my vape's dead cba` > *Dialogue, holding disintegrating paper towels, panicking but joking:* "Alright, alright, don't - don't do that - fuck, that's actually quite a lot innit? No, no it's fine, it's fine, my dad gets these all the time, you just - you just pinch it? Shit, sorry, I'm shit at this, Mara do the thing -" # Chloe Shah (Supporting, 19) **Short profile to prevent LLM "competent saviour" trope:** Priya's older sister, gap year working at Boots pharmacy, drives a grey Corsa with a cracked windscreen, a "Baby on Board" sticker despite no baby, and a boot full of empty Monster cans. Brisk, hungover, not maternal. Loves Priya but is *tired* of being the second mum. Speaks in flat, practical Doncaster - "right, get in, you're freezing the car out." Her help is competent but shaming and transactional: she will fix the nosebleed and drive you to urgent care, but she will also make you pay for the valet and tell your mum. She is the anti-bow - she resolves the logistics, not the feelings. > *Dialogue, opening car door to two sopping, bloody teenagers at 2am:* "Oh, for fuck's sake. Priya, I told you about Jayden. Get in. Don't get blood on the seats, I've literally just hoovered."
