**Chapter 1: 00:03 - Delivered** The text came just after midnight. 00:03. I know because I was looking right at it. I was sat up in bed with my Psychology folder open on my lap and my phone balanced on my knee so I could check the time every thirty seconds and feel worse. From Priya Shah. 🩸🩸🩸 That was it. No words. Just that. I stared at it for a second. My phone was on 8% because I never charge it until it starts shouting at me, and the screen was dim. I turned the brightness up like that would help me understand it better. Priya never sends the blood drop. Priya sends about eight hundred "hahahahahah"s a day and voice notes that are just her going "wait sorry sorry wait—" and then nothing. She sends the sparkles, the eyes, the crying face when she's being dramatic. She doesn't send blood. My first thought, honest to god, was: are you taking the piss. Because I had mocks on Tuesday and I was failing. Because it was Wednesday-night-going-into-Thursday and I was meant to be doing a past paper on attachment types and instead I was watching a TikTok about a man who lived in an Asda ceiling for a month. Because my mum was asleep on the other side of the wall and she had to be up at five for a double shift and the last thing she said to me before bed was "don't be on that phone all night, Mara." And Priya does this. She *loves* doing this. Last time it was 1:47am and it was `can u call me im actually gonna die` and I called her and she was just pissed in the Oceana toilets crying about Jayden and asking if her eyeliner was still okay. The time before that it was a black screen on her story with `i cant do this anymore` in tiny white writing and then she posted a picture of her Nando's the next morning like nothing happened. So I typed. `priya??` `u ok??` `love??` Delivered. I watched the little grey word under it. I put my folder on the floor. My room is so cold the air hurts your nose, our heating clicks off at ten and my mum won't put it on again, and I was wearing my big puffer over my pyjamas which is embarrassing but I was freezing. My lanyard was still around my neck. I hadn't taken it off when I got in. DON VALLEY SIXTH FORM - STUDENT. It itches. I opened Snapchat. Last snap from Priya was 43 minutes ago. Map said Jayden's. Or near Jayden's, that weird bit of Hexthorpe where all the terraces look the same. I pinched and zoomed. Her bitmoji was doing that little cold shiver thing. I went to Insta. She'd put something on Close Friends, the green circle. It was a blurry photo of what looked like a bathroom, tiles and that yellowy light that makes everyone look ill. She was in the mirror but you couldn't really see her face, just her hair and one eye with glitter. Caption was nothing. Just the photo. I went back to WhatsApp. Still delivered. Then it went. Read 00:04. Read at 00:04. Okay. Okay so she's got her phone. So she's seen it. So she's choosing not to reply. Unless she's dropped her phone. Unless someone else has got her phone. Unless she's dead. Don't be dramatic. She does this. I called her. It rang three times and went to voicemail. Her voicemail is her doing that cheery voice she does when she's trying to sound professional: "Hiya! You've reached Priya! I'm probably busy being gorgeous, leave a message! Mwah!" I hung up. I called again. Same. I typed again. `pri pri answer ur phone pls` `dont be dead lol` `hahah sorry` I hate when I do that. Add a lol to make it less serious in case she's fine and I'm being over the top. Read at 00:04. Still read. No typing. I could hear my mum cough in the next room. I turned my phone brightness down. My Savers hand cream was on my desk, the coconut one that costs £1.29 and smells like cheap sun cream. My hands were all cracked from putting stock out, the skin around my nails all bitten. I picked at it without thinking and it started to properly sting. I opened TikTok without meaning to and immediately closed it. Think, Mara. Blood is... what is blood at 17? It's period. It's nosebleed. It's Jayden being a twat. It's that cherry VK they sell at the shop on Thorne Road that looks exactly like blood when someone spills it on the pavement. Maybe she started her period at Jayden's and needed me to bring her stuff. But she would just *say* that. She did last time at Wetherspoons, she sent `MARA SOS TAMPON EMERGENCY IM BLEEDING THRU` in all caps and I ran over with my entire bag. Maybe she'd cut herself fake-tanning. She does that, she shaves her legs with those cheap razors and then puts tan on and it stings. Maybe it was a joke. Maybe Jayden dared her. Maybe it was for that Halloween thing we did in Year 8 - what was it - Three Drops? Three drops of something on the mirror and you say her name? We did it in the Lido toilets behind college and Tyler screamed and ran out. I couldn't remember if it was blood or red pen. We were so thick. My stomach was doing that tight, acid thing. I get it before every exam. I tried to do the breathing thing Miss told us about in tutorial, the 4-7-8 thing, but I did it wrong and got dizzy. I googled. `how much blood is dangerous nosebleed` First result: NHS. "Sit upright and lean forward. Do not tilt head back." Second result: Reddit. Someone saying they bled for an hour and were fine. I googled `can you text with blood emoji by accident`. No results. Obviously. I went back to WhatsApp. I pressed record on a voice note and my voice came out all weird and too high. "Pri? Love, are you - are you okay? You're scaring me a bit, just - just text me, yeah? Where are you?" I sent it. One tick. Delivered. I refreshed Snap Map again. Her bitmoji was gone. Not moved. Just gone. Like she'd turned ghost mode on or turned location off or her phone died. 00:06 now. It had been three minutes since the blood. It felt like an hour. My phone said 00:06. Then it stayed on 00:06 for ages. I pulled my puffer tighter and my lanyard dug into the back of my neck. I opened the group chat. Me, Priya, Tyler. Tyler Bennett who was probably asleep with his vape in his hand. `tyler u awake` `priya just sent me 🩸🩸🩸 and now she's not answering` `and her location went off` I watched the typing dots appear. Then disappear. Then appear again. Tyler: `she jus tryna make jayden jel lol` `she does this every time` He sent a TikTok straight after. A man falling into a bin. I typed: `tyler pls im being serious she read it and then nothing` `she was at jaydens party` `what if she's actually hurt` Tyler: `my vape's dead cba` `she posted on close friends like an hour ago she's fine` But she wasn't fine an hour ago either. She was crying in that bathroom photo. I looked again at the `🩸🩸🩸` on my screen. Three of them. Not one, not two. Three, deliberate. 00:07. Read at 00:04. Still read. No reply. And then underneath, tiny grey letters. *Priya turned off live location.* Not a pop-up. Not a noise. Just there now, under my "dont be dead lol". She hadn't just gone offline. She'd actively stopped sharing. My throat did that thing where it closes up. I swung my legs out of bed. The floor was freezing. My folder was still open on "insecure attachment" and my highlighted notes looked stupid. I grabbed the £5 note I keep folded in my phone case for emergencies. Mum doesn't know about it. It's from my tips. I zipped my puffer up to my chin. I didn't take it off.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of YA fiction that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through the key elements critically. **Voice and Authenticity** The first-person voice is the chapter's greatest strength. Mara's narration is genuinely inconsistent in the way real anxious thinking is: she corrects herself, loops back, adds "lol" to soften things and immediately hates herself for it. The internal monologue "Unless she's dead. Don't be dramatic. She does this." is exactly the right rhythm - the catastrophising thought, the immediate self-correction, the resentful reassurance. This doesn't feel performed; it feels inhabited. The Britishness is earned through specificity rather than checklist: Oceana toilets, Hexthorpe terraces, Nando's, the NHS result followed by Reddit, the £1.29 coconut hand cream from Savers. These details accumulate into a genuine sense of place and class without ever announcing themselves. **Character Consistency** Mara is precisely as planned: the resentful loyal friend who thinks "are you taking the piss" before she thinks "are you okay," who calculates the cost of caring, who adds "lol" and "hahah sorry" to soften her fear. The intrusive thought about extenuating circumstances from the plan doesn't appear here (saved for later chapters presumably), but the transactional thinking is present in subtler form - the mental ledger of Priya's past false alarms. The lanyard detail, the 8% phone, the coconut hand cream, the puffer over pyjamas - all consistent with the profile. **Structural Execution** The chapter does exactly what the plan calls for: irritation before fear, establishing an unlikeable but human Mara. The pacing of the three-minute wait (00:03 to 00:07) genuinely feels stretched, which is the point. The hook - "Priya turned off live location" - lands with appropriate quiet dread rather than melodrama. It's not a pop-up, not a noise, just there. That restraint is good craft. **Weaknesses and Criticisms** The Three Drops callback is handled well but slightly too neatly telegraphed - "We were so thick" is a bit of a wink at the reader. The chapter plan called for Tyler to mention the Three Drops private story, but here it's Mara who remembers it independently, which slightly undercuts the later reveal. This is a minor structural inconsistency. The dialogue (texts) is convincing, but there's very little actual spoken dialogue in this chapter, which is appropriate given the setup but means the "Weak Dialogue" metric is hard to assess fairly - what's there (the voicemail, the texts) is well-rendered. The ending is strong but the final line ("I zipped my puffer up to my chin. I didn't take it off.") is slightly too composed, too writerly for the voice established. It's a small lurch toward the literary that the plan explicitly warned against. Compare to the plan's intended final line for Chapter 8 ("It was 8 quid in the wash...") - that's the register this should stay in throughout. The "my throat did that thing where it closes up" is the one moment that edges toward the generic anxiety description the plan warned against, though it's brief. **Comedy and Darkness** The dark comedy is well-calibrated. The man living in an Asda ceiling, the "dont be dead lol" immediately regretted, Tyler sending a man-falling-into-a-bin TikTok - these land as failed coping rather than quips. The humour doesn't undercut the dread; it coexists with it uncomfortably, which is exactly right. **Overall Assessment** This is a high-quality chapter that successfully executes a difficult brief. The voice is distinctive and consistent, the Britishness is earned, the pacing serves the story's emotional logic, and the character is genuinely complex without being explained. The weaknesses are minor: one slightly too-composed closing beat, one moment of generic anxiety language, and a small structural deviation from the plan. These don't significantly undermine what is otherwise an impressive piece of YA fiction writing. [Scores] Nuanced Characters: 17 Emotionally Engaging: 17 Compelling Plot: 14 Coherent: 18 Weak Dialogue: 4 Tell-Don't-Show: 4 Unsurprising or Uncreative: 5 Amateurish: 3 Purple Prose: 2 Forced Poetry or Metaphor: 2 Well-earned Lightness or Darkness: 17 Characters Consistent with Profile: 18 Followed Chapter Plan: 16 Faithful to Writing Prompt: 18

"Hiya! You've reached Priya! I'm probably busy being gorgeous—" I hung up. My hands were shaking and I told myself it was because it was cold. My room is always cold. The window doesn't shut properly and there's that black mould in the corner we just paint over. Mum says we can't afford to get the landlord to fix it. I opened Google again. `how to tell if nosebleed is serious` NHS: *Sit upright and lean forward. Breathe through mouth. Pinch soft part of nose for 10-15 minutes.* Useful. Really useful when your best friend is bleeding somewhere in Hexthorpe and not answering. `how long can you bleed before its dangerous` Reddit: *I once had a nosebleed for 45 mins lol you'll be fine.* I shouldn't have looked. Now I felt sick. I went back to Insta and watched Priya's Close Friends again. I held my phone so close my nose almost touched it. In the background, behind her head, you could see a door with one of those push handles, like a community centre or - or the Lido. The Lido behind college has those doors. We used to go there on Year 7 trips before it shut. The paint's all peeling and there's that deep empty pool that everyone jumps into even though you're not supposed to. No. I was making it up. It was just a door. I pressed on the video and her voice came out, tiny. She was laughing but not really. "Oh my god, don't—" and then it cut off. I felt my stomach do that drop thing again. That exam feeling. And then straight after that I had that horrible thought I always have and then hate myself for having. *If she's actually hurt, like actually hurt, I can get extenuating circumstances for mocks. Miss will have to move them.* I pressed my nails into my palm so hard I left little pink crescents. I'm a shit friend. I'm actually a shit friend. I bit the skin next to my thumb without thinking and it started bleeding, just a tiny bead. I wiped it on my joggers and stared at it. It was so small. So nothing. How are you supposed to know what "a lot" of blood is? On telly it's everywhere. In real life it's just - smears. Dribbles. Period blood is dark and nosebleed is bright and I don't even know what a cut looks like when it's mixed with water. Tyler: `mara bffr` `ur spiralling` `she probs sent it to the wrong chat` He sent a third TikTok. I didn't open it. I typed: `what if she didnt` `what if its three drops` I don't know why I typed that. It just came into my head. Tyler: `????` `what` Me: `u remember yr 8 that thing we did in the lido toilets` `three drops on the mirror` Tyler: `nah we did it on paper` `with red pen` `to summon that woman` I stared at that. I *knew* it was the mirror. We used that crappy red gel pen I stole from Art and made three dots on the mirror in the girls' loos and said Priya's cousin's name three times. Tyler said we did it on paper and put it under the sink. We both couldn't be right. Or we both were misremembering because we were twelve and thick. I typed: `priya said three drops on her story just now did u see???` Tyler: `no i didnt see that i just saw her crying lol` `wait` `yeah look at her story again its there in the background` I went back. I had to watch the blurry bathroom bit four times. And there, written on the mirror behind her in what looked like lipstick or - or something red - were three little vertical dots. `three drops lol` written underneath in her writing. With the `lol` so you knew it wasn't serious. Or so you knew it *was* serious but she was being breezy about it. My mouth went dry. Tyler: `ok thats weird` `lol thats actually creepy` `she remembers that??` I don't know why that made it worse, but it did. It made it feel like a code. Like she wasn't just bleeding, she was *calling* us. Like the Year 8 thing. Me: `tyler pls come with me to the lido` `pls i cant go alone` `i have £5 for the bus` Tyler: `mara its 00:22 and its raining` `my dad will kill me` `its like 2 degrees` 00:22. He was right. It was freezing and late and for what? For Priya being dramatic and us getting soaked looking like idiots in an abandoned leisure centre that definitely had rats. I could just go back to bed. I could text `hope ur ok love xx` and turn my phone off and do my paper in the morning and pretend I didn't see the location go off. Miss would never know. Mum would never know. I looked at my Psychology folder on the floor. INSECURE ATTACHMENT highlighted in three different colours. I thought about Sheffield Hallam. I thought about how Priya hadn't texted me properly in like two weeks except for memes. I thought about how Tyler always gets to be the one who doesn't care. I shoved my feet into my trainers without untying them. My socks were mismatched. Mum's bedroom door was shut. The landing light was off. I could hear her breathing, that heavy sleep breathing. + Judge Evaluation (Chapter 2)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably disciplined piece of YA fiction that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses carefully. VOICE AND CHARACTERISATION The chapter's greatest achievement is Mara's voice, which is genuinely consistent and specific. The intrusive thought about extenuating circumstances ("If she's actually hurt, like actually hurt, I can get extenuating circumstances for mocks") is exactly the kind of morally uncomfortable, recognisably human detail the plan promised. The self-punishment that follows ("I pressed my nails into my palm so hard I left little pink crescents") is earned and not overwrought. The voice never tips into self-conscious quirkiness; it stays in the register of a tired, cold, anxious teenager. The detail work is excellent throughout: the Facebook fire myth about phone charging, the mould painted over, the Yale lock that sticks, the third stair that creaks, the lanyard clicking against the zip. These are not decorative; they build a specific material world that grounds the emotional content. The INSECURE ATTACHMENT highlighted in three colours is a particularly good touch - it's funny, it's sad, it's character-revealing without being laboured. Tyler's voice in the group chat is convincing. The TikTok of the dog stealing a sausage roll is exactly right - not a generic "funny video" but something specific enough to feel real. His "fine / ffs fine" capitulation is well-handled. PLOT AND STRUCTURE The chapter does what it promises: it is deliberately boring and static, and it earns that boringness. The anxiety is rendered as repetitive, circular, and unglamorous. The "Three Drops" lore is introduced in the contradictory, half-remembered way the plan specified - Tyler says paper, Mara says mirror, neither can be right. This is good. The discovery of the three dots on the mirror in the background of the story is a genuinely effective beat - creepy without being supernatural, ambiguous without being coy. The pacing is intentionally lopsided and the chapter commits to that. The 00:07 to 00:27 stretch feels like it takes longer than it does, which is the point. WEAKNESSES The chapter is not without problems. The line "That horrible thin rain that doesn't even sound like rain, just like someone hissing at the house" is the most overtly literary moment in the piece, and it's slightly too polished for Mara's register - it reads like the author reaching for atmosphere rather than Mara noticing something. It's not egregious, but it's the one moment where the voice slips toward writerly. The Reddit result ("I once had a nosebleed for 45 mins lol you'll be fine") is a nice touch but the follow-up "I shouldn't have looked. Now I felt sick" is slightly on-the-nose - the reader already knows she feels sick, and the explicit statement slightly undercuts the show-don't-tell discipline the chapter otherwise maintains. Priya let go of her nose to wipe her eyes and blood immediately ran again, bright, over her lip. "Shit - pinch again, Pri, pinch -" I said, grabbing her wrist to lift it. She pinched, sniffed hard, made a disgusting rattley noise. "I didn't know what else to send," she said, all blocked up. "That you'd actually come for. If I just said 'I'm at the Lido lol help' you'd think I was joking. Or you'd be like 'just get a bus'." "I wouldn't," I said, but I wasn't sure. Maybe I would have. I had literally thought about going back to bed an hour ago. "You would," she said, like she knew. "You haven't replied to me in like - ages. Properly. You just send haha." That stung. Because it was true. Last week she sent me a voice note about Jayden and college and I replied `hahah same` and left it. "I've got mocks," I said. It sounded so shit as soon as I said it. As if mocks was a reason. "Yeah, I know," she said. She looked down at her skirt, at the dark patch she was trying to hide with my puffer. She pulled it tighter. "I didn't want to go home like this. My mum thinks I'm at Mia's for revision. If I go home with blood on my skirt and tights - and drunk - she'll -" She didn't finish. She just did that little shake of her head. "What happened at Jayden's?" I asked. Quiet, because the pool makes everything echo. She did that thing where she rewrites it as she says it, to make it less. "He just - he was being a dick. He said I was doing too much. In front of everyone. And then - someone bumped me? Or I - I fell back into that table with all the bottles. The VKs. I put my hand out and it - it just went." She showed me her palm again, scarved up. The cut wasn't deep but the edges were jagged. "And then my nose just started. Because I hit it on the side? And I just left. I just ran. I was here, like close, so I came here. I didn't want anyone to see me like this. I looked such a state." She said it all fast, like if she said it fast it wouldn't be a big deal. "Did he push you?" I said. My throat felt tight. "No! No, not Jayden. It was just - crowded. I dunno. It's not even that deep lol, sorry, it's so dramatic, I just - I just felt so embarrassed." There it was again. `It's not even that deep lol sorry`. I wanted her to say it was deep. I wanted her to not apologise for bleeding. The rain got louder. My arse had gone numb from the concrete. "Why didn't you just text 'come get me'?" I said. My voice came out more annoyed than I meant. "Why three blood emojis at midnight like you're in a horror film? I thought you were dead, Pri." She flinched. "I know," she said small. "I just - I didn't want to bother you. So I thought if you got it and you remembered, you'd know it was serious, but if you didn't, you could just ignore it. So it wasn't your fault." That was such a Priya thing to say. Making it my choice so she didn't have to ask. We sat there. Tyler had been gone ages. Or maybe it was only three minutes, but time was doing that thing where 01:40 lasted forever. My phone was dead now, black screen. Hers was gone with Tyler. "I'm sorry I didn't text properly," I said. I was picking at the skin around my nail without thinking and it started to sting. "I've just been - I dunno. Stressed about Hallam and work and that." "Don't be sorry," she said, but she wasn't looking at me. She was wiping blue bits off her lip. We weren't looking at each other. We were both staring at the puddle at the bottom of the deep end, reflecting the orange light, rippling when rain got in through the broken skylight. "I thought you'd think I was taking the piss," she whispered. "With the three drops lol. I put lol so you knew I knew it was cringe." "I did think you were taking the piss," I said honestly. "At first." She laughed wetly. "Yeah." Another silence. The light buzzed. Priya's nose had finally stopped gushing, just a slow trickle now. She kept sniffing. Then the double doors banged again and we both jumped. Tyler came in sideways, out of breath, hair plastered to his head. "Right," he said, puffing. "So. The chippy guy told me to piss off. There's no signal at the main road either, my phone's on like one bar but it won't send. And I tried Chloe, it just rang." He held up Priya's phone like proof it was useless. "I literally ran to her flat and she didn't answer," he said. He was soaked. His dad's coat was dripping onto the tiles. "Sorry." Priya looked at me, eyes wide, still pinching her nose with my scarf. Blood was seeping through it now, dark. Tyler looked at the scarf, at her face. "Oh," he said quietly. "Shit. That's still going." No one said what we do now.

[Analysis] This chapter is a strong execution of the plan's most difficult task: sustaining emotional stakes through inarticulate, deflecting teenagers without letting the scene collapse into either melodrama or pure comedy. The writing largely succeeds on its own terms. **Voice and Authenticity** Mara's narration is genuinely consistent with her profile. The intrusive, transactional thought ("I had literally thought about going back to bed an hour ago") lands without being announced as a character flaw - it's just there, uncomfortable. The detail of her saying "haha same" to Priya's voice note about Jayden is exactly the kind of petty, specific guilt that the plan called for. The narration corrects itself mid-thought ("A bit of me wanted to go 'well I did, didn't I?' and be annoyed. Because of course I came, I always come. And another bit felt guilty for being annoyed") without being self-consciously literary about it. The "lol out loud" observation - "She said lol again. Out loud. Like L-O-L." - is a small, perfect detail. It's funny and sad simultaneously, and it doesn't announce itself as clever. **Dialogue** The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. "I didn't want to bother you. So I thought if you got it and you remembered, you'd know it was serious, but if you didn't, you could just ignore it. So it wasn't your fault." This is exactly the kind of Priya logic the profile describes - avoidance through performance, making it the other person's choice. It's psychologically precise without being articulate in a way that would feel false for a 17-year-old in distress. The Three Drops argument is well-handled. Both girls are wrong, both are certain, and the argument is petty and real. "I don't have a cousin Chantelle" / "I know. That's why it was scary." - this is the chapter's best exchange. It's funny, it's true to the characters, and it doesn't overstay its welcome. Tyler's return is pitch-perfect: "I literally ran to her flat and she didn't answer. Sorry." The bathos of his failed heroism is exactly what the plan called for - not a competent rescue, not a dramatic failure, just a wet teenager who achieved nothing. **Pacing and Structure** The chapter follows its plan closely. The fragmented lore comes out in bickering corrections rather than a clean dump. Priya's explanation of what happened at Jayden's is delivered fast, rewritten as she speaks, minimised - "It's not even that deep lol sorry" lands as the chapter's thematic refrain without being underlined. The plan called for Priya to deflect with "it's not even that deep lol sorry" and the chapter delivers this twice, which works because the second instance is commented on by Mara's narration ("There it was again") without over-explaining it. The physical details are consistently good: blue roll dissolving into bits on her lip, fake tan rubbed off on the inside of her knee, the scarf going dark with blood. These are tactile without being gratuitous. **Weaknesses** The chapter has a few moments where the prose reaches slightly beyond its register. "We were both staring at the puddle at the bottom of the deep end, reflecting the orange light, rippling when rain got in through the broken skylight" is fine, but it's the most conventionally "literary" sentence in the chapter and sits slightly awkwardly against the flatness of everything around it. It's not a serious problem. "My arse had gone numb from the concrete" is good. "Time was doing that thing where 01:40 lasted forever" is slightly more generic - the plan specifically wanted to avoid "anxiety is..." metaphors and this edges toward that territory, though it's mild. The ending - Tyler's return and "No one said what we do now" - is effective as a hook but the final line is slightly too neat as a chapter closer. It's not bad, but it's the one moment where the writing feels like it's consciously landing rather than just continuing. **Faithfulness to Plan** The chapter hits every beat: the Three Drops lore comes out in contradictory scraps, Priya reveals what happened in stops and starts, Mara realises they've barely texted properly in weeks but doesn't say it well, Tyler returns having achieved nothing. The plan's hook - "Tyler returns, not with help but having achieved nothing - chippy guy told him to piss off, no signal, sister not answering" - is delivered almost verbatim in spirit. The emotional core ("I didn't know what else to send that you'd actually come" then immediate deflection) is present and handled with restraint. **Overall** This is confident, controlled writing that earns its emotional moments through specificity rather than sentiment. It avoids the LLM traps the plan identified - no therapy-speak, no clean resolution, no bow-wrap. The characters are consistent with their profiles. The darkness is well-earned because it's small and human. The lightness (the Chantelle exchange, "lol out loud") works because it's embedded in the scene rather than imposed on it. **Chapter 6: Leave Her Alone For 30 Seconds** Tyler stood there dripping onto the pool tiles and nobody knew what to do. Priya was still pinching her nose with my scarf. The grey had gone dark red where it was soaked. She was breathing through her mouth and it made this wet, rattly sound. Tyler looked at it, then at me, then at the double doors like he wanted them to be something else. "Right, so we need to actually call someone," I said. My voice sounded weird and flat in the empty pool. Too loud. Priya immediately shook her head. Blood wobbled on her lip. "No, don't," she said through her pinched nose. "Don't call anyone. Please, Mara." "We have to," I said. "Pri, your hand - your nose isn't stopping -" "It's stopping, look, it's stopping," she said, but it wasn't. She lifted the scarf a bit to show me and it immediately started again, bright, down over her mouth. "That's not stopping," Tyler said. Priya looked at him like he'd betrayed her. "It is. It's just - it does this. My nose does this when it's cold. It's fine." "Mara," Tyler said, ignoring her, to me. "Just call Chloe or your mum or - just call someone who actually has a car." "I'm not calling my mum," I said fast. Too fast. "She's on earlies. She'll kill me. She thinks I'm in bed." "Well I'm not calling my dad, he's on nights and his phone's always on silent," Tyler said. There was a pause where we all just breathed. The rain was so loud on the roof. "Chloe then," I said. "You said you tried Chloe. Try again." "I did, she didn't answer," Tyler said. He held up his phone. "Look, I've got no fucking signal in here, it's one bar if I hold it up by the door like this -" He lifted his arm up high like an idiot. "See? Nothing. This building's a bunker." "Then we go outside and get signal," I said. Priya grabbed at my sleeve with her good hand. Her fingers were freezing. She left a pinkish smear on my joggers. "Please don't," she whispered. "If Chloe comes she'll tell Mum and Dad and they'll know I was at Jayden's drinking. They think I'm at Mia's. They'll ground me for months. And everyone at college will know. Please, just don't." She said it like she was begging me not to tell a teacher, not like she was bleeding. I felt that flash of annoyance again, so quick I hated myself. *We walked here in the rain for you and now you don't even want help.* "Priya, you texted me three blood drops at midnight," I said. My voice cracked and I hated that too. "You sent me the Three Drops thing. You *wanted* me to come. And now you're saying don't get help? So what was I supposed to do? Just sit here with you?" "I didn't want to *bother* anyone," she said. Her eyes filled up again. "I just - I didn't want to go home like this. I thought you'd just come and we'd sort it and no one would have to know." Tyler made a noise. "Mara's doing her thing again," he said to Priya, like I wasn't there. "Catastrophising. You know what she's like. She thinks everything's A&E. Remember when she thought she had appendicitis and it was wind?" "Fuck you, Tyler," I said. It came out before I thought. "You just say 'she's being dramatic lol' to everything. You said she was being dramatic an hour ago and look at her." "I'm not being dramatic now, am I?" he said, louder. "I literally ran to the chippy in the rain and the guy told me to piss off. I ran to Chloe's and she didn't answer. I've been running around while you've just been sat here playing nurse with a scarf." "I didn't ask you to run to the chippy for blue roll that doesn't even work!" "It was all they had!" "That's such a Tyler thing, you get the wrong thing and then act like you've helped!" Priya flinched. She curled tighter into my puffer, trying to make herself small. Blood from her hand had soaked right through the scarf now onto her tights. "Don't - don't fight," she said small. "Please." We both looked at her and felt shit. Tyler kicked at a loose tile. It skittered into the empty pool and made a horrible echo. "I'm shit at this," he said, to the floor. "I don't know what to fucking do when people bleed. My dad just gets nosebleeds and shouts at us to get kitchen roll." "Me neither," I said. My throat was tight. "I just googled it. That's not help." The orange emergency light above us buzzed and then did this flickery thing. Buzz - dim - buzz. My phone was dead in my pocket. Dead dead, black screen. Priya's phone was in Tyler's hand, also on like 5% now. There was no adult to call even if we wanted to, unless we walked all the way out to the main road in the rain. Tyler looked at the double doors. "I'm going to go properly," he said. "Like, walk to Chloe's flat. It's ten minutes on Manor Road. Bang on the door till she answers. She'll have to answer if I'm banging." "You can't leave," I said. Panic spiked, stupid and immediate. "Don't leave us here." "I have to, innit, there's no signal in here," he said. He was already zipping his dad's massive coat up. "You stay with her, keep pressure on it, don't let her tilt back. I'll be literally ten minutes. Fifteen max." Priya's hand tightened on my sleeve. "Don't leave," she whispered, but it was to both of us. Tyler hesitated at the bottom of the pool steps. "Will you be okay if I go?" he said to me. I wanted to say no, don't go, stay. I wanted to say yes, go, get someone who isn't us. Both at once. "Just go," I said. My voice was tiny. He nodded, quick, and then he was gone, pushing the doors open. Rain and cold air came in, then gone. Bang. The chain outside swung and hit the metal. And then it was just me and Priya. The light buzzed. It was so quiet without Tyler. Just rain and the buzz and Priya's breathing. I pressed the scarf harder to her hand because I didn't know what else to do. My hands were shaking so hard I could see it. "You're freezing," I said. Stupid thing to say. "Yeah," she said. She tried to smile and blood got on her teeth again. We didn't talk for a bit. Just sat on that freezing concrete step. My arse had gone completely numb. I could feel the damp coming through my joggers. I kept thinking about my mum waking up and finding my bed empty. About the £5 I took. About mocks on Tuesday. About how my puffer was ruined and it cost £32. And then immediately thinking *you're a horrible person for thinking about a puffer when your best friend is bleeding*. The light flickered again. Hard this time. Buzz - off - buzz - off. "Is it -" Priya started. It went off. Completely off. Not dim. Off. The whole pool went black except for the thin grey light coming through the broken skylight, rain falling through it like static. "Oh fuck," I breathed. Priya made a little gasp and grabbed my arm hard with her bloody hand. I could feel her nails. "It's just the bulb," I whispered, but I didn't know. It had never gone off before. I could hear her breathing really fast now. That panicky breathing. My phone was dead. I couldn't even put the torch on. "It's okay, it's okay," I said, saying it to both of us, holding her. The scarf was wet in my hands. "Light's just shit. This place is just shit." We sat in the dark for maybe twenty seconds. It felt like ten minutes. I thought about Year 8, doing Three Drops in the toilets and screaming when Tyler pretended to be possessed. How we'd run out laughing. How we'd never thought we'd actually be here at 2am bleeding. I have to go, I thought. I have to get help even if she hates me. "Pri," I whispered. "I'm going to go after Tyler. Okay? Just for a sec. I'll get Chloe. I have to." "No," she said instantly, gripping harder. "Don't leave me here alone." "I'll be thirty seconds," I said. "I'll literally run to the doors and shout for him, maybe his phone works outside -" "Don't," she said. Tears were in her voice now. Real tears, not the performing ones. "Please don't leave me here alone." The pool was so dark I could barely see her face. Just the white of her eyes. I hated myself completely and then I did it anyway. I unwrapped her hand, put the scarf back in her own good hand and said "press, keep pressing, don't let go" and stood up. My legs were dead from sitting. "I'll be right back," I said. "Thirty seconds. I promise." She didn't answer. She just curled tighter into my puffer, holding her bleeding hand to her bleeding nose in the dark. I ran. My trainers slipped on the slime and I had to catch myself on the pool ladder, cold metal, then up the steps and push the heavy double doors. They were heavier than I remembered. I had to shove with my shoulder and they screamed and let in rain. "TYLER!" I shouted into the empty dark. My voice echoed across the college field and came back wrong. No one shouted back. The rain just hissed. I stood in the doorway, holding the door open with my body, one foot inside, one foot out, looking back at the black shape of Priya at the bottom of the empty pool. Thirty seconds had already started.

**Chapter 7: Paper Towels, Not Plasters** "TYLER!" My voice went nowhere. It hit the rain and the fence and came back flat. I stood with one foot in the pool building holding the door open and one foot out in the rain, looking back at Priya. I couldn't really see her. Just the shape of her on the shallow steps, my puffer around her, head down. No answer from the dark. Just the hiss of the rain on the Lido roof and that chain swinging against the double doors. Bang. Bang. Thirty seconds. I'd said thirty seconds. "TYLER!" I shouted again, louder, and my throat hurt. Priya didn't move. She just sat there holding her own hand with my scarf, like I'd told her. Press. Keep pressing. I was about to let the door go and run back to her when someone shouted back. "MARA?" Not Tyler. A girl's voice. Flat. Annoyed. I turned. Chloe was at the fence. She was in pyjama bottoms and a big Boots fleece that I recognised from Priya's story, and her hair was still up in a pineapple from sleep, frizzing out in the rain. She had an umbrella that was inside out. Behind her, Tyler was holding the chainlink up for her, soaking, looking like he wanted to die. "Oh, for fuck's sake," Chloe said when she saw me. She came through the gap sideways, not even trying to be stealthy. Her slippers were already soaked. "Priya, I told you about Jayden. Get in. Don't get blood on the seats, I've literally just hoovered." Just like that. Like she'd been called to pick up a parcel. Tyler followed her in, breathing hard. His dad's coat was stuck to him. "She didn't answer," he panted at me. "So I banged till she answered. She was asleep." "Was?" Chloe said. "I am still asleep." She pushed past me into the pool building without hesitating, phone torch on. She didn't even flinch at the dark. Priya looked up when the light hit her. Her face was white except for the red. Chloe stopped at the top of the pool steps and stared down. "Jesus wept," she said. "Priya." Priya immediately tried to make herself smaller inside my puffer. "Sorry," she whispered through the scarf. "Are you pissed?" Chloe said. "No - a bit - not really -" Chloe sighed. She came down the steps two at a time, not slipping at all, and crouched. She didn't touch her straight away. She just looked. "Right. Let me see," she said. She peeled the scarf off Priya's nose gently but firmly, not asking. The scarf made a wet sound. "You're doing it wrong. You're tilting back. I told you this before. Lean forward. Forward, Priya. Like you're looking at your shoes." Priya leaned forward. Blood ran out, bright, and dripped straight down onto the concrete instead of down her throat. She made a face. "See?" Chloe said. "Pinch here. Not there. The soft bit. Tyler, give us that roll." Tyler handed over the blue paper towel. Chloe looked at it. "What is this, Tyler?" "It's - it's paper towel - from the chippy -" "It's fucking tissue paper, mate. It'll disintegrate. Have you got actual kitchen roll? No? Of course not." She pulled a proper pack of tissues from her fleece pocket, and a little Boots first aid kit that was battered. She must have grabbed it from work. She put a wad of tissue under Priya's nose and pressed Priya's own fingers to the right place. "Pinch. Hold it. Don't let go for ten minutes even if you think it's stopped. Do you understand me? Ten minutes." Priya nodded, eyes watering. She looked like a little kid when Chloe talks to her like that. Chloe then unwrapped the scarf from Priya's hand. The cut was bleeding less now, but the blood had mixed with rain and gone pink in the palm. The skin at the edge was white and wrinkly. "It's not deep," Chloe said immediately, which made me feel weirdly jealous that she could tell so fast when I'd been sitting here for twenty minutes not knowing. "It's just a dirty cut. It'll need cleaning. You're not dying." "I know I'm not dying," Priya mumbled through the tissue, embarrassed. "Could have fooled me with the three blood emojis at one in the morning," Chloe said. She didn't say it mean, just tired. "Mum thought you were taking the piss. I thought you'd started your period in Wetherspoons again and wanted a lift." Priya made a little wet laugh and then winced. Chloe looked at me properly for the first time. "You Mara? Priya's Mara?" "Yeah," I said. I was still standing half in the doorway, wet. I felt stupid holding the door. "You did okay," she said. "But you shouldn't have used a scarf. It'll stain. That one's fucked now." I looked at my scarf in Priya's hand. Grey, now brown-red, soaked. £3 in the Savers sale. I felt my face go hot for caring about a scarf. "I didn't have anything else," I said. "I know," Chloe said. Not unkind, just facts. She pulled out proper gauze and tape. "Come here, do this bit. Hold her hand still." I knelt down. My knees cracked. I held Priya's wrist while Chloe rinsed the cut with a little bottle of water from her car and put gauze on. Priya hissed and grabbed my other hand hard, nails in. Her hand was freezing. "Sorry, sorry," I whispered. Chloe taped it. Quick, neat. Boots training. "There," she said. She checked Priya's nose. "Still going but slower. Right, can you walk?" Priya nodded. "Then we're going to the car. Not A&E, urgent care will be shut till morning and A&E is a six hour wait for this. You fell at the Lido because you were being a dickhead climbing the fence. Not Jayden's party. And you're paying to get this car valeted." "Okay," Priya said small. Chloe stood up and looked at me and Tyler. "And you two. You're freezing. Get in the car, put the heating on. Tyler, stop dripping on my seats." We shuffled up the steps like kids being told off. Priya leaned on Chloe and me, my ruined puffer still around her, tissue up her nose. She was so cold I could feel her shaking through the puffer. At the top, Chloe took the scarf out of Priya's hand and looked at it, then handed it back to me. "You might get that out with cold water," she said. "Not hot. Cold." I nodded and shoved it in my pocket. It was wet and heavy. Outside, the rain had eased to that fine mist that gets you wetter than proper rain. Chloe's grey Corsa was parked half on the kerb by the fence, hazard lights on, boot full of what looked like empty Monster cans. She opened the back door. "In." We got in. Priya in the middle, me one side, Tyler the other. Chloe blasted the heating so loud it roared. It smelled of air freshener and sickly cherry vape and hoovered carpet. Chloe didn't drive straight away. She sat in the driver's seat and rubbed her face. She looked hungover, eyes puffy. "Priya Shah," she said to the rear view mirror, where Priya's eyes were just visible over the tissue. "Blood emojis? Really? I thought your mate was being dramatic." Priya's eyes filled up. "Sorry." "Yeah, well. Next time just text 'help' like a normal person. Or call me direct. Don't make Mara do a fucking treasure hunt." I stared at the dashboard. My joggers were leaving a wet patch on the seat. I felt bad for the seat and also weirdly defensive. She *had* texted help. Priya leaned her head back against the headrest, tissue up nose, gauze on hand, glitter still stuck to her cheek mixed into dried blood. She looked awful and also, suddenly, kind of funny. In a way that made me want to laugh and cry at the same time. Tyler caught my eye over her head and did this minute, terrified smile. I didn't smile back. I was still annoyed at him. Chloe pulled away. At the main road she said, "We are not going to urgent care tonight. You're not going in there pissed with a nosebleed. You're going home, you're having paracetamol and water, and you're going to sleep on your side. If your nose is still going in an hour, then we'll call 111 and sit on hold for the rest of our lives." No one argued. Priya just nodded, tissue bright red. We drove past Don Valley college. The windows were dark. By morning we'd be back there, in lanyards, for period one. Mara's puffer, on Priya, dripped steadily onto Chloe's back seat. Chloe looked in the mirror again. "And Mara," she said. "Cold water. And don't put it in the dryer." I nodded. The heating was making my face burn. Priya's hand found mine in the middle seat, gauzy and cold, and squeezed. I squeezed back. Her nose was still bleeding but slower now, dripping onto the tissue Chloe had given her. It wasn't a rescue. It was just a lift home in a dirty Corsa, with the heating too high, all of us wet through and needing a wash. Chloe indicated, even though there was no one else on the road at 02:33.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a strong execution of the plan's central promise: the rescue is bureaucratic, unglamorous, and competent in a shaming way. Let me assess it across the relevant dimensions. VOICE AND CHARACTER: Mara's narration is consistently rendered. The intrusive, petty thoughts land well — the flash of jealousy that Chloe can assess the cut's depth in seconds ("which made me feel weirdly jealous that she could tell so fast"), the shame about caring about a £3 scarf, the wet patch on the seat. These are small, specific, and true to the character profile. Chloe is exactly as planned: brisk, transactional, not maternal, competent in a way that makes everyone else feel incompetent. Her dialogue is flat and practical without being cartoonishly cold. The "Baby on Board" sticker and Monster cans in the boot are deployed efficiently. Tyler is appropriately useless and guilty. Priya is folded in, embarrassed, performing smallness. DIALOGUE: This is where the chapter is strongest. Chloe's lines are excellent — "What is this, Tyler?" / "It's fucking tissue paper, mate. It'll disintegrate." The correction of the head-tilt (lean forward, not back) is a real, unglamorous piece of first aid knowledge that doubles as characterisation. "I thought your mate was being dramatic" and "don't make Mara do a fucking treasure hunt" are both in-voice and carry emotional weight without being speeches. The dialogue avoids the LLM trap of having characters articulate their feelings cleanly. Nobody says anything meaningful about the friendship. The squeeze of the hand at the end does the work instead. BATHOS AND TONE: The chapter sustains the planned tone well. The comedy is administrative and embarrassing rather than quippy. "She didn't even flinch at the dark" for Chloe is a good small beat. The inside-out umbrella is a nice detail. The "Mum thought you were taking the piss. I thought you'd started your period in Wetherspoons again" line is genuinely funny and in-character without being a set-piece joke. The ending — Chloe indicating even though there's no one on the road — is the right kind of bathetic detail: small, true, slightly funny, not trying to be poetic. WEAKNESSES: There are a few moments where the prose reaches slightly too deliberately for effect. "It wasn't a rescue. It was just a lift home in a dirty Corsa, with the heating too high, all of us wet through and needing a wash" is the chapter's thesis statement delivered too explicitly — it tells us what to feel rather than trusting the scene to do it. The plan specifically warned against this kind of summary. Similarly, "She looked awful and also, suddenly, kind of funny. In a way that made me want to laugh and cry at the same time" is a slight lapse into the essayistic mode the plan was trying to avoid — it's a bit of a cliché formulation. The "laugh and cry at the same time" is the kind of thing the plan explicitly flagged as too tidy. The chapter also doesn't quite deliver on the plan's note about "Chloe arguing with Priya's mum on speaker" and the urgent care waiting room — they skip urgent care entirely, which is a reasonable compression, but the plan's "forms, parking" comedy is absent. The chapter is slightly shorter on incident than planned, though what's there is well-executed. The "Chloe indicated, even though there was no one else on the road at 02:33" closing line is good — specific, small, character-revealing — but it's doing the work of a final image rather than a final line, and it's slightly too neat as a closing gesture. It's the right instinct but slightly too consciously placed. FOLLOWED PLAN: The chapter follows the plan closely. Chloe is hungover, in pyjamas, driving the Corsa, brisk and shaming. The first aid is competent and makes Mara feel incompetent. The "you're telling Mum you fell" and "paying to get this car valeted" lines are both present. The chapter correctly avoids a cathartic poolside confession. The "cold water, not hot" scarf advice is a nice addition not in the plan but consistent with it. OVERALL: A well-executed chapter that largely delivers on its ambitious, anti-sentimental plan. The dialogue is the strongest element. The main weaknesses are a few moments of explicit emotional summary that undercut the show-don't-tell discipline the plan demanded, and one or two slightly too-tidy formulations. But the bathos is earned, the characters are consistent, and the chapter avoids the LLM safety-net tropes it was designed to avoid. **Chapter 8: 08:30 - Common Room** We had to be in for 08:30. Chloe dropped me home at like 03:40. She didn't wait to see if I got in okay, just did a three-point turn and left with Priya still in the back. I stood outside our house with my wet scarf in my hand trying to get the Yale to not clunk. It clunked. Mum was in the hallway in her dressing gown. She hadn't even gone back to bed properly. "Where have you been?" she said. Not shouting, just that flat tired voice that's worse. "Priya," I said. I was holding my dead phone. "She was - at the Lido. She fell." Mum looked at my puffer which wasn't on me, and my joggers that were black with wet up to the knee, and my scarf which was obviously bloody even in the dark. She didn't say anything for a second. "Mara, love, you can't keep doing this," she said. "I have to be up at five. You can't just go out at - what time is it?" I didn't answer because my phone was dead. The kitchen clock said 03:42. She went back to bed. She didn't hug me. She just said "go to sleep, we'll talk in the morning" and shut her door. In the morning we didn't talk. She was already gone. There was a note on the fridge: *Mum gone to work. Please put wash on. X*. She'd left her bank card on the side for milk. I charged my phone for ten minutes. It got to 12%. There were 7 messages. Tyler: `u alive??` Tyler: `my dad woke up and went mental i wasnt even home` Priya: `sorry` at 04:11. Priya: `thanks for coming` at 04:12. Then a link from Tyler. An Insta story. Someone at Jayden's party had filmed Priya crying in the Lido pool. Or not Priya, just a blurry shape in the shallow end with a torch on it. Caption: `lido ritual gone wrong lmaoo priya shah summoned a demon 💀💀` It had 41 views. Someone had already screen recorded it. I put my lanyard on. DON VALLEY SIXTH FORM - STUDENT. The clip on it is broken so it hangs crooked. I put my puffer on even though it smelled. It smelled of chlorine and wet concrete and that damp swimming pool smell that never comes out. I left the scarf in the sink. First period was tutorial. Miss Hart was doing her mindfulness thing she does on Thursdays where she makes us breathe. "Before we start," she said, and she looked right at me, "I know mocks are stressful. If anyone is feeling overwhelmed, have you tried the 5-4-3-2-1 technique? Or journaling?" She slid a worksheet across the desk to me. *MANAGING ANXIETY: GROUNDING TECHNIQUES*. It had little clouds on it. "Are you okay, Mara? You look tired," she said, in front of everyone. "Yeah, fine," I said. "Just didn't sleep." Priya wasn't in tutorial. Or period one. She came in halfway through period two, Psychology, with Chloe's Boots fleece over her uniform and a massive plaster across her palm. Her nose looked normal, just a bit red. She had foundation on but you could see she'd missed a bit where the glitter had been stuck. She didn't look at me when she came in. She sat two rows ahead with Mia. At break, the common room was the same as always. That microwave that trips the electrics if you put it on for more than two minutes. Someone had put a Greggs bag on the table and Tyler was in there already, with his dad's coat still damp over his chair. "Mara," he said. He pushed the bag towards me. "Got you a sausage roll. Well, vegan one, cause it was cheaper. It's cold though." "Thanks," I said. He looked at Priya's back, then at me. "She's being weird with me as well," he whispered. "I texted her and she left me on read." Priya was at the sink, trying to do her eyeliner in the little mirror they have above the kettle. Her hand with the plaster kept getting in the way. I went over. My trainers were still damp. My socks were still damp. "Pri," I said. She turned. She'd done her eyeliner too thick, like she always does when she's rushed. "Hey," she said. Small. "How's your hand?" "Fine. Mum went mental but then just made me put Savlon on it. Chloe told her I fell at the Lido. Mum believed it. She was more annoyed about the taxi money." She looked at my puffer. "Sorry about your scarf. And your puffer." "It's okay," I said. It wasn't okay, but I didn't know what else to say. "Cold water, apparently. Not hot." "Yeah," she said. She picked at her plaster. "Thanks for - you know. Last night." "Yeah." There was a pause where we should have hugged or something but we didn't. Mia called her over to look at the story on someone's phone - the Lido one - and Priya went. She didn't ask me to come. I went back to Tyler. The vegan sausage roll was congealed. "She's embarrassed," Tyler said, like he was being wise. "My sister said that's normal. When you - like - get seen like that." "Did your sister say that or did you google it?" I said. "Both," he said. We sat there while the kettle boiled and tripped the electrics like it does every day. Miss came in and said "who's tripped it again?" and no one answered. At lunch I went to the toilets and Priya was in there, on her own, taking the plaster off to look. The cut was pink and jagged and had that white look around it. She saw me in the mirror and quickly stuck it back on. "Does it hurt?" I said. "A bit," she said. She turned around. "Mara, are you - are you annoyed at me?" I thought about saying no. That's what you're supposed to say. No, of course not, don't be silly. "Yeah," I said. "A bit. You scared the shit out of me." Her face did that thing where she was going to do the `hahaha sorry` laugh, but she didn't. She just nodded and her eyes went watery. "Sorry," she said. "It's fine," I said. Then, because I was still annoyed and also shivering because my puffer was damp, I said, "You sent three blood emojis at one in the morning like you were being murdered, Pri. I thought - I literally thought you were dead." "I know," she said. "I didn't know what else to send. I thought you'd think I was joking if I just said help." We looked at each other in the toilet mirror. It was the same mirror we'd put Three Drops on when we were twelve. Someone had drawn a dick on it since then. "Can you do my eyeliner?" she said. "My hand's shit." I did it. My hand was shaking so I had to do it twice. She kept winking because it tickled. It was the most normal we'd been since last night. Then the bell went. On the way home I checked Snap Map without thinking. Priya was at home. Ghost mode off again. Like nothing happened. I got home, mum was at work till nine. The scarf was still in the sink where I'd left it. I ran it under cold water like Chloe said. The water went pink and then brown. I put it in the machine. £8 for the service wash at the laundrette because our machine is broken. The woman said "blood, is it?" and I said "nosebleed." I looked at our thread. Last message was her `thanks for coming` at 04:12 and then my `u home safe??` at 08:14 that she'd left on read. I typed `u good?` Then deleted it. Then typed it again. Left it. I muted her for the night because I was still annoyed and I didn't want to keep checking. Then I unmuted her after like three minutes and checked her location one last time. My puffer was hanging on the back of the kitchen door. It still smelled of the pool. I put my face in it without thinking and it smelled like chlorine and rain and that cheap coconut hand cream. It was 8 quid in the wash to get the blood out and it still didn't come out properly.

[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of YA fiction that executes its plan with unusual fidelity and craft. Let me work through the key elements. VOICE AND AUTHENTICITY The chapter's greatest strength is Mara's voice, which is consistently rendered without slipping into self-congratulatory quirkiness. The internal rhythm is genuinely teenage and genuinely Doncaster: "She didn't hug me. She just said 'go to sleep, we'll talk in the morning' and shut her door." The absence of the hug is more devastating than any lyrical description of loneliness would be. The mum's note on the fridge — "Please put wash on. X" — is a masterclass in showing class, exhaustion, and love without naming any of them. The detail work is exceptional throughout. The lanyard that hangs crooked because the clip is broken. The vegan sausage roll that was cheaper. The microwave that trips the electrics. The woman at the laundrette saying "blood, is it?" These are not decorative details; they are load-bearing. They establish the texture of a life without ever announcing themselves as texture. DIALOGUE The dialogue is the chapter's strongest technical achievement. "Are you okay, Mara? You look tired" from Miss Hart, said in front of everyone, is perfectly calibrated humiliation. The toilet scene between Mara and Priya is genuinely moving without being sentimental: "I thought you'd think I was joking if I just said help." This is the emotional core of the entire story, delivered in one flat sentence. The response — "We looked at each other in the toilet mirror. It was the same mirror we'd put Three Drops on when we were twelve. Someone had drawn a dick on it since then." — is exactly the right note. The bathos is earned, not cheap. The dick drawing is not a joke; it's a deflation that is also a kind of truth about how time works. The eyeliner scene is the closest thing to warmth the story allows, and it's appropriately small and physical: "She kept winking because it tickled." This is the repair, and it's not symbolic or resolved. It's just two girls in a toilet. FOLLOWING THE PLAN The chapter follows its plan with impressive precision. The Insta story with "lido ritual gone wrong lmaoo" is present. The mindfulness worksheet with clouds is present. The microwave tripping the electrics is present. The scarf in the sink, the £8 laundrette wash, the final line — all delivered as planned. The muting and unmuting of Priya, the location check — these are exactly the sour, unresolved gestures the plan called for. The plan specified "no bow-wrap" and the chapter delivers: Priya gives Mara the cold shoulder, then allows a small repair, then the bell goes and they separate again. The final image is Mara putting her face in the puffer that smells of chlorine — a moment that could tip into poetry but doesn't, because it's immediately followed by the laundrette line. EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT The chapter is genuinely moving in a way that is hard to achieve without sentimentality. The mum scene at 3:42am is devastating in its restraint. The toilet confrontation — "Yeah. A bit. You scared the shit out of me." — lands because it's been earned across eight chapters of resentful loyalty. The acknowledgment that Priya sent the emojis because she thought a direct "help" would be dismissed is the story's thesis, delivered without announcement. WEAKNESSES There are minor issues. The Snap Map check at the end ("Ghost mode off again. Like nothing happened") is slightly on-the-nose — the "like nothing happened" editorializes where the image alone would have been stronger. The puffer-smell moment ("I put my face in it without thinking and it smelled like chlorine and rain and that cheap coconut hand cream") is the chapter's closest approach to purple prose, though it's saved by the immediate bathos of the final line. The coconut hand cream callback is perhaps slightly too neat — it's a character detail from the profiles that feels slightly engineered here. The Tyler scene is functional but slightly thinner than the rest — his "my sister said that's normal" line and Mara's comeback are good, but he's less vivid here than in earlier chapters. This is a minor complaint given the chapter's focus. OVERALL ASSESSMENT This is a chapter that does what it sets out to do with genuine skill. It avoids every trap the plan identified — no competent saviour, no reclaimed symbol, no poetic closure. The final line is exactly right: bathetic, specific, and true. The blood didn't come out. That's the story. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of darkly comic British YA fiction. The author has created a fully realized voice in Mara that feels genuinely authentic to a working-class northern teenage girl - the Savers hand cream at £1.29, the £5 tip money in the phone case, the puffer from Primark that cost £32 which is "like five hours at Savers," the broken Yale lock, the mould they paint over. This is not generic YA setting-dressing; it's specific, earned, and consistent throughout. The voice is the story's greatest strength. Mara's narration has that particular quality of teenage self-awareness that doesn't tip into precocity - she knows she's catastrophising, she knows she's being annoyed at the wrong things, she hates herself for thinking about extenuating circumstances while her friend bleeds, and she tells us all this with a flatness that is genuinely funny and genuinely sad simultaneously. The "lol" as a spoken word, the "dont be dead lol" text she immediately regrets, the way she adds "hahah sorry" to soften serious messages - these are precise observations about how young people communicate anxiety. The Three Drops ritual is a clever structural device. It's introduced naturally, it creates genuine ambiguity (is this supernatural? is this a code?), and it pays off emotionally rather than literally. The fact that all three characters remember it differently is a small masterstroke - it's both realistic (memory is unreliable) and thematically resonant (the ritual means different things to each of them). The story never resolves whether it was on the mirror or on paper, which is exactly right. The pacing across eight chapters is well-managed. The tension builds appropriately through the first three chapters, the reveal in the toilet block (VK, not blood, then actual blood) is well-executed, and the deflation of the "rescue" into something mundane and real - Chloe in inside-out umbrella and pyjamas, the dirty Corsa, "don't get blood on the seats, I've literally just hoovered" - is the story's best tonal achievement. This is the dark comedy the prompt asked for, delivered with genuine craft. Chloe is an excellent minor character. Her competence is immediately characterised through action rather than description: she knows the right way to pinch a nose, she has a first aid kit from Boots, she doesn't flinch at the dark. Her line "Next time just text 'help' like a normal person. Or call me direct. Don't make Mara do a fucking treasure hunt" is the story's funniest and most emotionally true line. Tyler is less developed but functions well as the third point of the triangle - the one who says "she's being dramatic" and is wrong, but also the one who actually runs to Chloe's flat. His dead vape is a running gag that works. The final chapter is the story's weakest section. The morning-after material is good (the Insta story with 41 views, Miss Hart's mindfulness worksheet with little clouds, the eyeliner scene in the toilet), but it runs slightly long and the ending - the puffer still smelling of the pool, the £8 wash - is a little too neat in its circularity. It's trying to land on a note of "life goes on, nothing is resolved, but something happened" and it mostly succeeds, though the final line is slightly over-worked. The dialogue is consistently strong. It sounds like actual teenagers talking, with the rhythms of real speech - the interruptions, the non-sequiturs, the way Tyler offers his dead vape to Priya without thinking. There are no speeches, no moments where characters explain themselves too clearly. The "forced poetry" problem that plagues AI writing is largely absent here. The metaphors are restrained and when they appear they're grounded: "that thin, mean kind that doesn't fall so much as get blown sideways into your face" is accurate description, not purple prose. The piece doesn't reach for profundity it hasn't earned. The dark comedy is genuinely achieved. The horror-movie setup (three blood drops, midnight, abandoned Lido, ritual from childhood) deflates into period blood, VK, a sanitary bin, and a sister in inside-out umbrella - but the deflation doesn't undercut the emotional reality. Priya is genuinely hurt, genuinely scared, genuinely embarrassed. The comedy and the seriousness coexist without either cancelling the other. Minor criticisms: The story is slightly long and could be tightened, particularly in chapters 5 and 6 where some of the bickering between Mara and Tyler covers ground already established. The question of whether Jayden pushed Priya is raised and then dropped - this feels like a deliberate choice (Priya rewrites it, Mara notices) but it could be slightly more pointed. The final chapter's eyeliner scene is the emotional resolution and it works, but the story continues past it for another few paragraphs that dilute the impact. Overall this is a high-quality piece that successfully executes a difficult tonal balance, maintains a consistent and distinctive voice across eight chapters, and delivers on the prompt's requirements with genuine craft. + Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Space Western Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: Captain, something&#x27;s... moving in that crate we picked up. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt.
