**Chapter 2: The First Cut** The fog came down at noon and didn't lift. It wasn't like regular fog. It was yellow-grey and low, and it smelled like the greenhouse did when it went white. Sweet and dirty. The spore counter Lena left us last spring would have been ticking but hers broke in July and we never fixed it. You could just see it. The air got thick. Dust in the sunbeam thick. That means nobody goes outside. Not without a mask and we don't have filters anymore. Two days, maybe three, then the wind takes it. It got stuck at 3pm. I was re-taping the door when I heard it. Not a knock. A drag. Like someone pulling their feet. It was small. High school kid. Grey hoodie, the kind with the string. Snow up to its shins and it couldn't lift its feet right, so it just shuffled into the snowbank by the propane tank and got stuck. It stood there, breathing. Wet inhale. Wet exhale. The caps on its face were smaller than the man's yesterday. Buttons, pale, clustered around its mouth and eyes. You could still see the mouth. You could still see it was a kid. Jun was at the table. He went small. Knees up. He didn't cry, he just watched me. "It's stuck," he whispered. "I see it." It wasn't leaving. It kept trying to step and falling a little forward, hands out. It made a sound. Not a word. Just air through wet mushroom. If it stayed there it would call others. They come to the breathing. And when the fog lifted, we'd have a trail right to our door. I got the axe. The fire axe from the hall, the one Tomas showed me how to hold. Jun said, "Don't go out." "I'm not going out," I said. I opened the door six inches. Cold and that sweet fog poured in. I had my shirt pulled up over my nose. It did nothing. It was three feet away. Hood up, head down. I could see the crown of its head where the hair was still hair, then the skin broke into that ruffled white. Snow melting off its shoulders. I swung. I was prep, not line. I never learned how to break down anything bigger than a chicken. I hit the neck but not clean. The blade stuck. It wasn't like meat. It gave like wet wood. Milky fluid jumped out and the smell hit me even through my shirt. Not rot. Loam and yeast. Fresh bread from the kitchen at Blue Star when they proofed the rolls. And underneath, like turned earth. It dropped to its knees. It didn't scream. It just exhaled, hard, and a puff of that yellow dust came out of the caps on its cheek. I stepped back and slammed the door and kept slamming until the axe came free. We stood there both breathing. Jun was crying now without sound. I re-taped the door with shaking hands. Warm the tape. Press it hard. "It's okay," I said. Too loud. "It's okay, it left. It left." It didn't leave. It was right there, on the other side of the wall, on its side in the snowbank. I could see its shoe through the gap under the door. One sneaker. White. The fog got thicker after. You couldn't see the woodpile. We ate the last beans for dinner. Half portion. I cut them smaller so it looked more. Jun ate his and asked for more and I said that's the trick, kiddo, always leave a little hungry, that's what Chef says. He didn't understand. He chewed his cuff. Propane at maybe an eighth now. I didn't mark it. At night the wind came but the fog stayed. The thing outside breathed. I could hear it through the wall. Slow. Wet. Jun woke up at 1am crying because his stomach hurt from being empty. Then at 2am. Then at 3. "My tummy is empty empty," he said. He was in the big quilt, shivering even though the stove was on. His face was all chapped. "It hurts." "I know," I said. I rubbed his back. My hands were cold. "I know, kiddo. Sleep." He didn't sleep. He just whined, that low kid whine that gets inside your teeth. At 3:30 I got up. I don't know why. I just couldn't listen to it anymore. I put my boots on. I pulled my shirt over my face. I opened the door. The cold hit my legs. The fog was still there, sour and sweet. The kid was right where it fell, on its side, hood still up. Eyes open but capped over, white. Snow had covered one leg. The fluid around its neck had gone dark and tacky. It had stopped breathing. I dragged it by the hoodie onto the little concrete porch. It was lighter than I expected. Like it was hollow. Jun called from inside, "Mara?" "Stay inside," I said. My voice cracked. "Tape the door." I had no oil. No butter. Nothing. But I had the pan. I tapped it twice without thinking. I knelt. I wiped my little prep knife on my thigh. I picked the calf. It looked the most like meat. The skin there had split and underneath the flesh was layered, creamy white and pale pink, fibrous, like king oyster mushrooms pulled apart. It smelled... Christ, it smelled good. Like when you slice a fresh button mushroom and there's that clean, meaty smell. And pork fat. I cut a piece the size of my palm. The flesh squeaked against the blade. It twitched. I told myself it was just the fibers tightening. I went inside. I put the pan on the stove dry. No oil, no salt. I was shaking so bad the piece jumped when I dropped it in. It seared. It spat. The fibers tightened and curled. White juice came out and browned. The smell filled the whole break room immediately — pork, butter, earth. My mouth watered so fast it hurt and I hated that it did. I flipped it with my fingers. Burned them. Didn't care. I ate it standing over the stove. It was salty. Rubbery. Gritty, like there was still snow in it. I chewed and it squeaked between my teeth like undercooked mushroom and the fat coated my mouth, sweet. I swallowed half and the other half I had to force down. My throat did that thing before you puke. I leaned over the sink and vomited. Hard. Sour beans and bile and that white meat, mostly whole. Then I had diarrhea. I had to run to the bucket in the corner and squat and Jun turned to face the wall like I taught him. My face was burning. I wiped with the last of the newspaper. I expected to die. I sat on the floor with my back to the stove, shirt still over my nose, waiting for my throat to close or the caps to grow in my mouth. This is how people go, I thought. Stupid. Eating poison because you couldn't listen to a kid cry for one more hour. Jun whispered, "Are you sick?" "No," I said. "Just bad food. Go to sleep." I left the rest of the meat in the pan. I didn't cover it. I woke up on the floor. Sun through the window. The fog was gone. I wasn't dead. My stomach didn't hurt. I felt warm. Actually warm, for the first time in weeks, like I'd slept under a real blanket. And I was starving. Not empty-hurts starving. Hungry. The good kind, like before lunch rush. The pan was still on the stove. The piece I'd seared had gone cold and the fat had set white around the edges. It smelled like fresh bread and pork crackling. Like the best thing I'd ever cooked. My mouth watered again. From the porch I could hear the snow melting off the roof, dripping.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 2 executes its plan with considerable discipline and craft. The writing follows the chapter blueprint closely: the spore fog trapping them, the teenager in the hoodie getting stuck, the kill, the botched first consumption, the vomiting and diarrhea, and the morning-after revelation of hunger and the meat's renewed appeal. The prose is controlled and largely avoids the pitfalls the plan warned against. Sentences are short and functional under stress. "It gave like wet wood" is a precise, earned comparison. "Milky fluid jumped out and the smell hit me even through my shirt. Not rot. Loam and yeast. Fresh bread from the kitchen at Blue Star when they proofed the rolls." This is the plan's "disgust + deliciousness simultaneously" executed well — the smell is appetizing and wrong at the same time, and the Blue Star callback grounds it in Mara's specific history without being heavy-handed. The characterization of Mara is consistent with her profile. The compulsive re-taping, the "I tapped it twice without thinking," the knife wiped on the thigh — these behavioral tics are embedded naturally, not announced. Her internal voice is appropriately flat and self-justifying: "I told myself it was just the fibers tightening." The plan called for minimizing and self-justification, and it's here without being labeled. Jun's characterization is also faithful. He goes small, knees up. He doesn't cry until later. "My tummy is empty empty" is a child's phrasing, not a precocious apocalypse kid's. His turning to face the wall during Mara's illness — because she taught him to — is a small, devastating detail that shows their established domestic routine without explaining it. The horror of the kill is handled with restraint. The axe not going clean, the "wet wood" resistance, the puff of yellow dust from the cheek caps — these are specific and physical without being gratuitously gory. The sneaker visible under the door is an excellent, understated image. The ending is strong. Waking on the floor, not dead, warm for the first time in weeks, and then the hunger — "Not empty-hurts starving. Hungry. The good kind, like before lunch rush." This is exactly the seduction the plan called for, and the final image of the cold fat set white around the edges of the pan, smelling like the best thing she'd ever cooked, lands without being overwritten. Weaknesses: The dialogue is minimal and functional, which is appropriate, but "It's okay, it left. It left." is slightly on-the-nose as a self-deception moment — the plan's voice notes suggest Mara's self-justification should be more compulsive and specific. The line "This is how people go, I thought. Stupid." is the closest the chapter comes to telling rather than showing her fear, though it's brief. The fog description at the opening ("Sweet and dirty") is slightly generic compared to the more specific sensory work later. The "Chef says" line Mara uses with Jun feels slightly off — she was prep, not line, and the plan specifies she resents the chef; using "Chef" as an authority figure in a comforting lie is interesting but could have been shaded with more of her specific resentment. The chapter avoids purple prose almost entirely. There are no thesaurus words, no triple-adjective stacks, no em-dash aphorisms. The one moment that risks over-poeticizing — "My mouth watered so fast it hurt and I hated that it did" — is actually precise and earned, capturing the involuntary betrayal of appetite. Overall this is a well-executed chapter that serves the plan faithfully, maintains voice consistency, and delivers the promised "botched transgression" without sanitizing it or rushing to the reward. I started thinking like I was back on prep. Not surviving. Prepping. We had enough salt for one more cure. Enough vinegar if I watered it. The kid on the porch still had meat on it - shoulder, back. I told myself I was hunting because we needed it. That was true. But also I liked how the broth had been *good.* Like actually good, not just not-dead. Jun said it was like chicken. He asked for it. I wanted to do it again and have someone say I did it right. On the third day a big one came through. Older woman. Puffy parka, the shiny kind, pink. She was taller than the kid. She came slow down the old service road, snow up over her boots, breathing that wet inhale-exhale. The caps on her were different - not frilly oysters, but thick, round things the color of bruises, clustered on her neck and hands. They didn't quiver. They looked hard. She saw the break room. Or smelled the heat. She came right up to the south window and put a hand on the glass. The caps on her knuckles were cracked open and dust fell off. Jun hid behind the table. "Don't look," I told him. I got the axe. My mouth was dry but not the bad kind. The other kind, like before you flip a ticket. I opened the door. Cold bit my ankles. She was right there. I could see her face through the caps. Old, maybe sixty. Her eyes were still eyes, cloudy, but looking at me. She made a sound that was almost a word. I swung. Same spot. Neck. I put my back into it this time, so I wouldn't have to hit twice. It went in with a crunch, not a give. The blade stuck harder than with the kid. Fluid came but darker, brownish. And the smell - right away it was wrong. Not bread and earth. Bitter. Chemical. Like when the fryer oil goes off and you keep using it anyway, that fishy liver smell. It caught at the back of my throat. She went down heavy, on her knees, then face-forward in the snow. The parka hissed. I dragged her to the porch with the kid. She was heavy. I had to sit and pull by the sleeves. My shirt over my nose did nothing. The bitter smell got in my mouth. Jun was at the door, holding the tape. "You got another woods pork?" he asked. He said it like I taught him. He didn't sound excited. "Yeah, kiddo," I said. I was breathing hard. "Big one. Lots of meat." I let her sit out there an hour while I talked myself into it. Big, I thought. More fat. Maybe the bitter would cook out. Acid and salt fix bitter. That's what you do with greens. I wiped my knife on my thigh and cut into the thigh. The flesh was not creamy and pink. It was darker, grey-pink, and it didn't come apart in clean fibers. It was mushy in the middle and the juice that came out was brown and thin. The smell got worse when I opened it. Like bad liver left in a hot car. I cut anyway. Two pounds. I shouldn't have. I knew but I did it because I'd already killed her and propaine was burning. I did the same cure. Salt - I used almost the rest of the jam jar, my hand shook. Vinegar brine, water. Packed it tight. Waited six hours instead of twelve because I was impatient and Jun was asking when dinner was and I wanted to show him I could do it again. I rinsed it. Put snow water and the last bouillon cube in the pot. Put the meat in cold, turned it low. The same way. It didn't turn milky. The water went grey, then greenish. Fat came up but it was grey too, not yellow. And the smell filled the cabin so fast Jun gagged. I kept the heat on. I told myself it just needed time. It didn't. At ten minutes the stink was everywhere. Bitter, hot, metallic. Like burned hair and bad meat. Jun pulled the quilt over his nose. "It smells bad," he whispered. I stirred it. The fibers didn't pull tender. They stayed tough and then fell apart into mush when I poked them. I lifted a piece out, blew on it, tasted it because I had to know. It was so bitter my jaw locked. Not salty bitter. Poison bitter, the kind that makes your tongue go numb at the back. I spit it into the sink. My eyes watered. I spat again. The taste stayed. I gagged. I threw up over the sink, just bile and water, hard and fast. Jun cried out and I waved my hand, "I'm fine, I'm fine," but my throat was burning. I killed the stove. I grabbed the pot and threw it outside, threw the whole thing off the porch into the snow, meat and water and all. It hissed. The stink stayed inside. I had to air the cabin. That was the thing you're never supposed to do when the air is yellow. But I couldn't breathe in there. I opened the south window two inches and the door a crack. Cold and sweet fog poured in even though there was no fog that day, just the everyday spore haze you pretend isn't there. I stood in it with my shirt over my mouth, holding Jun's face into the quilt so he wouldn't breathe it. Ten minutes. I counted. My eyes burned. Then I closed everything and re-taped. The tape wouldn't stick at all because my hands were sweaty and cold. I had to hold it. Propane down to almost nothing. The scratch I made on the gauge was a lie now. I'd burned thirty minutes for poison. Jun sat at the table, pale. He'd had diarrhea again that morning, even though he only had a little broth. He didn't want any more. "It wasn't chicken," he said quietly. Not mean. Just true. I knew he was right and I hated that he was right. I scrubbed the pot with snow and the stiff brush until my knuckles went white. I scrubbed so hard the plywood cutting board slipped and I banged my hand on the table. I started crying. Not big. Just tears while I scrubbed, angry at the pan, at the woman in the pink parka wasting my salt, at myself for thinking I was good at this. "Sorry," Jun said right away. "Sorry, Mara." "Not your fault," I said, wiping my face on my sleeve. It left a salty smear. "This one was bad. Like a bad potato. You get bad ones. You just throw them out. That's prep. You don't use the bad potato." He nodded even though he didn't understand. When the cabin aired out a little, I went back onto the porch. The kid was still there under snow, the calf open and the meat gone grey at the edges but still okay. The woman was there too, steaming slightly in the cold. I left her. I cut the last good piece off the kid's shoulder. Smaller now, maybe a pound. Fibers still clean, cream and pink. It squeaked the same. It smelled like bread. I did the salt right this time. Less rush. I didn't use vinegar because we had almost none left. Just salt and low heat later. I saved it. Inside, Jun lined his stones up again, fast, clicking them. He put the bottle cap in the wrong order and fixed it, fixed it, fixed it. I tapped the empty pot twice before I put it down and my hand was shaking so bad I hit the rim wrong.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter executes its stated purpose with considerable skill: it breaks the progression established in Chapter 3, demonstrates failure and luck, and refuses to let the "farming is logical" arc feel inevitable. The plan called for spending word count on cleaning and failure rather than triumph, and the chapter delivers exactly that. The prose is disciplined and specific throughout. "Like when the fryer oil goes off and you keep using it anyway, that fishy liver smell" is exactly the kind of prep-cook knowledge the character profile demands — partial, embodied, self-serving. The detail of the grey-green water, the mush that won't pull tender, the jaw-locking bitterness — these are earned sensory details, not decorative ones. The chapter avoids the purple prose trap almost entirely. Mara's voice is consistent with her profile. The score-keeping mentality ("propane down to almost nothing"), the self-justification ("acid and salt fix bitter, that's what you do with greens"), the compulsive scrubbing while crying — all of these track precisely with the established character. The moment where she admits she wanted to do it again because Jun said she did it right is a small, devastating piece of self-knowledge that the character immediately moves past, which is exactly right for her psychology. The dialogue is sparse but functional. Jun's "It wasn't chicken" — "Not mean. Just true" — is the chapter's best line. It does real work: it shows Jun's literal sensory mode, his unfiltered honesty, and the way his honesty functions as criticism Mara can't argue with. Tomas's "You got talent, mija" from the character profile doesn't appear here (different chapter), but the dialogue that does appear is appropriately minimal and character-consistent. The chapter's structural choice — ending not with triumph but with Mara going back to the first corpse for the last good piece — is quietly excellent. It shows the precariousness the plan demanded without editorializing. The final image of her hand shaking so badly she hits the rim wrong is a good physical anchor. Some minor weaknesses: The opening two paragraphs ("Not just full. Warm. Like my blood was thicker.") are slightly too neat in their setup of confidence-before-fall. The transition from "I started thinking like I was back on prep" to the hunt is efficient but the motivation section ("I told myself I was hunting because we needed it. That was true. But also...") is slightly more explicit than the character's self-awareness usually allows — she's a bit too lucid about her own vanity here. The plan called for her to be more compulsive and less self-aware. The vomiting scene is handled well — quick, physical, not dwelt upon — and the decision to air the cabin despite the spore fog is a good practical horror beat that shows real cost without melodrama. The ending with Jun fixing his stones "fast, clicking them" and Mara's hand shaking on the pot rim is appropriately unresolved and embodied. The chapter doesn't wrap anything up, which is correct. One small craft issue: "She went down heavy, on her knees, then face-forward in the snow. The parka hissed." The parka hissing is a nice detail but slightly unexplained — it reads as atmospheric rather than grounded. Minor. Overall this is a strong chapter that follows its plan faithfully, maintains character consistency, and achieves its horror through specificity and failure rather than spectacle. The restraint is genuine, not performed. **Chapter 5: The Pantry Pet** By December the snow was up to the windowsills. You couldn't see the kid or the woman on the porch anymore. Just lumps under white. I stopped checking if they smelled. Cold keeps. Salt was almost gone. Just the bottom of the jam jar, crusty and damp. The rice was gone. We'd been on the good meat from the kid for ten days, small pieces, broth stretched with snow water. It was white and thin now but Jun still called it chicken so I kept calling it that. Propane was on fumes. The gauge needle sits under the scratch. I run the stove five minutes at a time and then turn it off and let the leftover heat do the work. I count. One broth for kid, one for me, five minutes, off. It was the woodpile that gave it to me. I went out to get an armful — quick, shirt over nose, no mask — and it was there, stuck between the logs and the cabin wall where the snow drifts. Not big like the man or the woman. Small. Maybe four feet. It was sitting, not standing. Pale all over, no jacket, no clothes except a piece of striped shirt stuck to its back. Caps hadn't opened yet. Just smooth, domed buttons, white as fat, clustered on its shoulders and head. Its face was still mostly a face. A boy. Young, maybe ten. Mouth open, breathing wet but quieter than the others. Thin arms. It didn't lunge. It tried to lift its hand and couldn't. Stuck. The snow around it had melted in a circle from its heat. Jun was in the doorway holding the door, not supposed to be. "Don't touch it," he said. I didn't. I stood there with wood in my arms watching it mew. That sound again, air through wet mushroom, but small. Like Jun when he has a cold. I should have hit it with the axe. That's what you do. You don't let them sit. I thought about dragging it to the porch and opening it like the kid. But I was so tired. And the meat from a fresh kill is better. The kid meat was getting grey at the edges even in the cold. This one was fresh and it wasn't going anywhere on its own. And I thought, if I keep it cold and dark it'll keep. Like mushrooms do. You keep them damp. I didn't think it all the way through. I just acted. "Jun, get the orange cord," I said. The extension cord. He didn't move. "Why?" "Just get it." He went. I put the wood down. I slipped the cord around the small one's chest, under its arms. It was light. The skin where I touched it was damp and gave a little, like the veil on a portobello. It smelled like earth and like kid sweat. I dragged it. It didn't fight. It made that small mew and its feet dragged. Snow melting off it left a wet trail. I pulled it through the door while Jun held it open with one hand, the other hand chewed at his cuff. "Mara, no," he whispered. "Don't bring it inside." "Not inside," I said. Loud and bright again, that fake voice. "In the pantry. Where it's cold. It's just a mushroom, kiddo. Not a person. See? It's just buttons." The break room has a root cellar. It's really just a concrete pit under the floor with a trap door, where they kept potatoes before. One foot deep, dirt floor. It's always damp and smells like cement and rot. Jun is scared of it. I opened the trap door. Cold air came up. I lowered it down. It was short enough to sit. I looped the cord around the old pipe bracket so it could sit but not stand up. I covered it with the blue tarp we use for wood. Not tight. Just dark and damp. It sat there breathing. Wet inhale, wet exhale. The sound came up through the floor. Jun stared down. "Why is it breathing?" he asked. "They all breathe," I said. I wiped my knife on my thigh even though I hadn't cut. "It's okay. Sleep. It's just in the pantry now." I gave it snow in a bowl. It didn't drink. I threw the last potato peelings down there. They went white and fuzzy by morning and it had grown over them a little. Threads. Two days later I checked. I lifted the tarp with my shirt over my nose and the boy was still sitting, head down. But on its back, where the striped shirt was stuck, the buttons had swelled. One shelf, flat and frilly at the edge, creamy white, maybe as big as my hand. It had grown right out of the shoulder, pushing the shirt aside. It looked exactly like an oyster mushroom. The ones we used to get in plastic at the store. I shouldn't have been excited. I was. I wiped my knife and cut it off, low, close to the base. The flesh squeaked. Milky juice beaded. The boy twitched but didn't make a sound. The stump wept a little and then stopped. I took it upstairs. While I was cutting, I was talking like I was on line, to nobody. "One harvest, slice thin, fry hard, keep the stump clean, keep it dark," I said. We had no oil except the very last scrape of margarine I was saving. I put it in the pan anyway. Tapped the pan twice. The margarine foamed and then the slices went in. Thin. They curled immediately. Browned at the edges in a way the corpse meat never did, because they were alive an hour ago. The smell was insane. Clean. Nutty, like browned butter and fresh mushroom and pig fat all at once. No bitter. No rot. I put one slice on Jun's tin plate and three on mine. The big ones for me. I told myself it was because I'm bigger. Jun ate his standing up, far from the trap door. "It doesn't squeak," he said. I ate mine. It didn't squeak either. It was tender, it gave between the teeth and the fat coated my tongue, sweet. I closed my eyes. After the grey broth this was like real food again, like a meal I might have paid for. "Good?" I asked. He nodded but he didn't ask for more. He went and lined his stones up, fast, clicking them. He put the smooth fungus piece at the end, facing away from the cellar door. That night he had a nightmare. He cried out, "Don't cut it," and I held him. He was sweaty. When he settled he said, very clear, "I don't like the pet. It breathes like you when you sleep. Can we not go down?" "It's not a pet," I said, too quick. "It's a garden. Like the potatoes. We keep it dark so it grows. That's all." He fell back asleep with his boots on. After, I went down again. I needed to see if the stump was okay. I told myself that. I sat on the cold concrete with my legs over the edge of the pit, feet not quite reaching the dirt. The boy breathed. I breathed. Cold bit my palms where I put them flat on the floor. I liked it. The sweet earth smell down here was stronger, it wasn't bad anymore. It was calm. I lifted the tarp a little. The stump where I cut was already filming over with white threads. Regrowing. I should have felt scared. I felt proud. Look, I thought. I kept us from starving. I got it to grow. I covered it back over, dark and damp, the way you're supposed to. Outside the snow kept falling, covering the porch again. Inside the cabin was warm enough with the trap door closed.

**Chapter 6: The Change** I ate the fresh ones for a week. A slice every three days. That's how long it took to grow back. I would lift the tarp and it would be there, flat and creamy, pushing out from the same spot on its back. I cut it low with my little knife, wiped the juice on my thigh, and covered it again. He had diarrhea on and off even from a little bit. I didn't anymore. Not at all. That was the first thing I should have noticed. I never get constipated. But after a week I was going less and when I did it was dark and it didn't smell bad. It smelled like the cellar. Like earth. I washed my hands twice after. The second thing was sweat. We don't wash much, just snow water on a rag. On the fifth day I did my armpits and the rag came away with a sweet smell even before I washed. Not body odor. Sweet, loamy, like when you break a fresh mushroom open. I sniffed it without thinking and then scrubbed harder. I didn't tell Jun. The cut on my thumb did it. I slipped while trimming a shelf. Tiny cut on the knuckle, just a bead of blood. I put pressure with my thumb, the way you do. Next morning I went to tape the window and the cut was closed. Not scabbed. Closed. There was a thin white line over it, like a thread caught under the skin. I picked at it with my nail and it didn't hurt. It came away like a little filament. Underneath the skin was pale and smooth, a little shiny. I wrapped it with tape anyway and said nothing. I started liking the cellar. Not just checking. Sitting. After Jun went to sleep I would open the trap door and sit on the edge with my legs hanging down, feet not touching the dirt. The cold coming up bit my palms when I put them flat on the concrete. I liked it. The breathing down there was slow. Inhale. Exhale. Wet but quiet. It matched mine if I stayed long enough. My mouth would water down there even before I cut anything. Like my body knew. Jun found me like that on the sixth night. He stood in the doorway in the big quilt. "Why are you sitting there?" he asked. "Just checking the temp," I said. My voice was flat in the cold. "Too warm it won't grow." He came and sat next to me even though I could tell he didn't want to. He copied me, hands flat on the concrete. He sniffed his own hands after and made a face. "You smell sweet," he said to me. Not mean. Just saying it. "Like the pantry." I pulled my hands back. "It's the mushrooms," I said. He nodded and went back to bed with his boots on. He didn't take his stones off the sill anymore. He moved them to the other wall, away from the trap door. The rice ran out on day seven. Not that we had rice, but the memory of it. I found a handful I'd spilled behind the locker, dusty. I rinsed it and boiled it for Jun, plain, to give his stomach a break. I tried a spoonful. It was like paper. No, like chewing on the tape. It had no taste at all until I swallowed and then it was just grit. I spat it into the sink when he wasn't looking. After that everything that wasn't the fresh slice tasted like that. The bouillon water. Snow. Even the salt if I licked my finger. Only the fresh slices tasted like anything. And they tasted more each time. The browning got deeper, the fat sweeter on my tongue. I closed my eyes every time. I coughed on the seventh night. Not a sick cough. Just a tickle. I was sitting at the table after Jun was asleep, tapping the pan even though there was nothing in it. I coughed into my hand. A puff came out. In the stove light I could see it, glittering, yellow-grey. It didn't burn going out. It felt good coming out, like I'd been holding my breath and finally let it go. Sweet. I stared at my palm. Little dust. I wiped it on my pants. I should have been terrified. I know that now. At the time I just thought, huh. And then I thought, oh. I was stirring snow water for Jun's morning wash and the thought came in with the steam, like it was part of it. What if the good ones are good on purpose? Like berries. Birds eat berries and shit the seeds and that's how the plant moves. Tasty so you carry it. I said it out loud because I was alone and the radio was just static. "Tasty so you carry it," I whispered. I looked at the trap door. The breathing came up through the cracks. I covered the water and didn't say it again. I didn't need to say it again. I cut a new slice that evening, even though the last stump hadn't fully grown back and was still thin at the edge. I fried it dark and ate it standing up at the stove before Jun could ask for any. He watched me eat from the cot. He didn't ask. He sniffed the air and then sniffed his own sleeve, the way I had. The counter Lena left us was in the corner. Tomas gave it to me before they left last spring, said crank it if the fog comes. I hadn't cranked it in weeks. That night I cranked it. It clicked. Slow, steady. Not fast like danger. Just... there. Ticking like a clock. I covered it with the quilt and went and sat in the cellar for a while, because it was the only place the ticking softened. Pale and damp and growing. That's what it wanted. Pale and damp and growing.

**Chapter 8: The Feast** They left at first light. I woke up before Jun. Lena was already folding her scarf. Tomas was lacing his boots. They hadn't slept much, I could tell by the way the quilt was still creased where they sat. I sat up. My mouth tasted sweet, like I'd been breathing cellar air all night. The trap door was closed and the quilt was over it, but I could still hear that faint wet inhale underneath. Lena saw I was awake and crouched next to the cot so we wouldn't wake Jun. "Storm's holding," she whispered. "If we go now we make the ridge by dark. Mara, come with us. We mean it. Tomas can pull Jun on the tarp if the snow's deep." Behind her Tomas nodded. He had his gloves in his hands, turning them. "We'd have to leave the wood," I said. It was the first thing that came out. Stupid. "We have wood stacked." "You have a spore farm under your floor," Lena said, not unkind. Very quiet and flat, nurse voice. "I know you think it's keeping you alive. It's also filling his lungs. Look at him." Jun was asleep in the too-big jacket quilt, mouth open, hair over his ears, boots off for once. He breathed fine. He looked pale the way he always looks in winter. Lena put her hand on my arm. Her fingers were cold. "You don't have to do this alone to prove you're good at it," she said. "You are good at it. You kept him alive when nobody else could. Now let us help." I felt that flash again, hot in my chest. Possessive. Be prep again. Be the one who needs help. Watch someone else feed him flour bread and take credit. "He is alive," I said. I pulled my arm back. "He's not hungry. You ate it last night, you said it was good. You wept." "We did," Tomas said over her shoulder. "It was good, mija. Best I've had. That's why we're scared." Jun stirred then. He sat up, quilt falling off. He saw Tomas with his gloves and Lena with her pack and his face did something. He looked at me. "Are we going to the flour place?" he asked. I should have said yes. "No, kiddo," I said. "We're staying. Our fire's here. Our stones are here." Jun didn't cry. He just looked down at his hands and picked at his cuff. Lena looked at me for a second longer, like she wanted to say something else, then decided not to. She reaches her limit fast, that's her thing. She left the spore counter on the table. The hand-crank one, grey plastic, with the little needle. She'd wiped it with her evaporated sanitizer out of habit. "Crank it once a day," she said. "If it clicks fast, get out. Even without masks. Okay? Promise me you crank it." I didn't promise. I just took it and put it on the sill next to Jun's stones so I wouldn't have to hold it. Tomas zipped his coat. He looked at the trap door one more time. "You keep it damp it'll rot your floor," he said to me, practical to the end. "That's concrete rot." Then they opened the door. Cold and clean winter air came in, not yellow, just normal cold that makes your teeth hurt. They stepped out onto snow that came to their shins. Tomas went first, breaking trail. Lena followed, then looked back once. "Keep the tape tight," she said. Then she pulled her scarf up and they went. I stood in the door with my shirt over my nose even though there was no fog. Jun came and stood next to me but didn't take my hand. We watched them until the brake and the airy blackness of the pine trees. [The trees swallowed them. ]() The snow where they'd stood melted a little from their heat and then refroze. I closed the door and retaped it. The tape didn't stick. I warmed it with my hands and pressed hard until my thumbs ached. It held for a second then peeled at the corner. I left it. "He's strong, he can carry you," Jun said, very quiet. Not accusing. Just saying it. "Forty miles." "I know," I said. "I counted." We didn't talk about it again. At noon I decided on the feast. Not because we needed it that day — the last shelf had only grown back thin — but because the cabin was too quiet after they left. I did it properly. Like I'd always wanted to on line. I lifted the tarp. The boy was still sitting, head down, orange cord slack now because it's learned not to pull. The stump where I'd cut was filming over with white threads again, regrowing even thin. I cut what was there, maybe half a hand, thin at the edge. Juice beaded milky. It twitched less now. I covered it dark and damp, the way you're supposed to. I put the pan on. I tapped it twice. It was a habit now, Jun did it without thinking too when he moved his mug. Dry pan, no margarine left, no oil. It didn't need it. The slices went in and immediately sweated clear fat that foamed. They curled and browned at the edges the way real meat does when you don't touch it too early. The smell - I know I've written it before but it was still that - pig fat and brown butter and mushroom and that sweet earth. It filled the break room and for a second it wasn't the break room with the sagging ceiling. It was warm. I set the table. That sounds fancy but it was the folding table with the book under the leg. I put the blue mug in the middle even though we weren't drinking from it, just because it looks right. I tucked the big quilt around Jun's shoulders where he sat on the chair so he wouldn't be cold. "You get the big one today," I told him. I meant it. I gave him the thick middle slice. I kept a thinner one for me, then changed my mind and swapped them when he wasn't looking. Old habit. We ate with our fingers because forks are cold. He took a bite and didn't say it squeaked. He chewed slower now, like he'd learned how. He closed his eyes for a second the way I do. "Good chicken," he said, because I call it that. "Good woods pork," I said, and tried to laugh the way I'm supposed to. It came out short. I took a big bite. The fat coated my mouth, sweet and salty, and the meat gave clean between my teeth. My shoulders dropped. Heat went down my neck to my hands. It was that same calm, full feeling, like after a long shift when you finally sit. Mid-chew my tongue found something loose. My left molar, top. It had ached a little last week but I ignored it. Now it moved. I wiggled it with my tongue and it came out. No pain. No blood. I took it out of my mouth and put it on the plywood next to the pan. It wasn't white like a tooth. The root was laced with fine threads, white, like the stuff that grows over the peelings in the cellar. They were still a little wet. I stared at it. Jun didn't notice. He was looking at his stones on the other wall. I picked the tooth up and set it beside the blue mug, crown up, like you would set a stone. I didn't wipe it. I kept eating. The bite after tasted even sweeter. After, when the plates were empty and greasy, I tried the snow water to rinse my mouth. It tasted like paper, like the rice. No taste at all. I spat it into the sink and it was just cold grit. Jun was full and sleepy. He leaned against me and I put my arm around him and his hair smelled sweet too, faintly. Like mine. The counter on the sill was where Lena left it. I cranked it like she said, once around. The handle was stiff from cold. It clicked. Slow, steady. Not fast. Just there, like a clock ticking. Click. Click. Click. In the warm cabin with the stove going and the greasy pan between us. I didn't cover it. I left it ticking. Under the floor the boy breathed. Inhale. Exhale. Wet and quiet. Regrowing. I tapped the empty pan twice and pulled the quilt tighter around Jun so the heat stayed in.
