**Chapter 1: Transfer Vessel *Clarity*** The transfer vessel *Clarity* rattled. That was the main thing. Not the view. Arthur Neegan had expected a view. Instead there was a jump-seat that was too small, a harness that cut into his shoulders, and a vibration that came up through the deck and into his teeth. The ship smelled of hot bakelite and old sweat and the chemical tang of the oxygen candles. An analogue altimeter ticked down above his head, needle jumping. He kept his hands on his knees. The dust was still in the seams of his boots. Martian orbit came up fast and mean below the port. Not the posters from the Arequipa training films. No grandeur. Just rust and rock and the long, flat shadow of Tharsis. His plot was down there somewhere. Dome 7-B, Claim 7-B. He couldn't pick it out. From up here it was all the same. He wondered, with a dull, delayed thud, what he had gotten himself involved in. He had run the tape twice. Forty thousand tons. Ninety-nine point eight percent. He had not wanted to run it a third time. At 05:30 that morning the dogs had not barked because there were no dogs. The pressure door had chimed. Arthur had been at the galley table, watering his coffee to make it last, his slide rule out. Mara was already up, wiping the filter housing. Jalen was still in his bunk. The chime was polite. Then the outer door cycled. Three men in dove-grey suits. Vacuum suits, but clean, pressed, city-clean. The insignia on the shoulder was an enamelled dove carrying a little gold orbit - the Antares Diplomatic Corps. The lead man was big and blocky, crew cut, sidearm set at the same angle as his leg. He held a clipboard. "Mr. Arthur Neegan?" the big one said. "Lease-holder, Claim 7-B, Tharsis Fringe Dome Association." Arthur stood up. His hand went automatically to straighten his shirt. "That's me." "I am Commander Voss, Antares Diplomatic Corps. High Commissioner Shah has politely requested your presence off-world for a meeting. We are here to invite you." The word invite did a strange thing in the room. Voss said it like it was printed on the form. Behind Voss, the other two did not point rifles. They didn't need to. They stood by the door at parade rest and looked at nothing in particular. One of them glanced at Mara and then away. Voss put the clipboard on Arthur's table, next to the coffee. There was a form on it, already stamped. "This is to confirm you are not being coerced," Voss said. "Please sign." Arthur looked at the form. Then at the sidearm. Voss, as if remembering his manual, lifted the sidearm very slightly off his hip and placed it on the table so Arthur could see it clearly. He did it helpfully. "We are not coercing you, sir," Voss said. Mara made a small sound. Jalen had come to the doorway of the bunk room, barefoot, hair flat on one side. He said nothing. He had learned not to make eye contact with men like that at all. "Where?" Arthur said. "The orbital station *Tamerlane*," Voss said. "High Commissioner Shah will explain. It concerns your recent assay. You are required to bring your copy for verification." Arthur's hand went to his pocket. The seismograph tape was there, folded. 40,000 tons. He had told himself it was a miscalibration. Voss, while Arthur signed, did an inventory. That was the procedure. He walked the hab slowly, looking at everything and writing it down. He stopped at the recycler housing. "Model C," Voss said, flatly. "Permit expired 09/14. That's a violation, sir. For your awareness." It had expired. Arthur knew it had expired. The filter was running at 112% to make up for it and Mara had been nursing it for a month. "Your charter review is due," Voss said, making a note. "High Commissioner Shah is concerned about air and water compliance. This meeting will be helpful for that." He said it without a threat. He didn't need to add one. Arthur had signed. The pen had left a dent in the paper because he was pressing too hard. They let him put his boots on. They let him bring his jacket. They did not let him bring his rock shelf. He looked back once as they walked him to the hopper outside - Mara with her hands held tight together, Jalen staring at the floor. He wanted to say something decent and paternal about looking after the hab while he was gone. What came out was, "Don't touch the geophone." Now the *Clarity* lurched. Something clanked in the bulkhead. The pilot, a kid in the same dove-grey, didn't look back. "Brace for spin-dock, sir." They weren't under arrest. That was in the wording of the form. Voluntary attendance. Invite. But the harness was tight and there was a man on either side of him who had not spoken the whole ascent. Arthur's shoulders ached. He was fifty-seven and thick through the middle now, gone soft where the suit used to be tight. The dust was ground so deep into his knuckles it never came out, no matter how he scrubbed. He squinted out the port again. Forty thousand tons. He'd drilled that ground for fourteen years and pulled nothing but ilmenite and dirty ice, just enough to keep the lease current. 7-B was supposed to be barren. That's why it had been cheap after Liora died. Now the tape said there was more Azra under his one small claim than the whole Tharsis Combined had pulled last year. Azra made slow atoms fast. That was what the manual said, one sentence. The rest was logistics numbers Arthur only half understood. But everyone understood what it meant: drives and weapons. If you had Azra you went interstellar. If the other fellow had it and you didn't, you didn't go anywhere ever again. That was the gold rush. That was the arms race. And somehow his bad ground was in the middle of it. The tape in his pocket was folded into a square so small it cut into his palm. He had run the geophone array himself. He tapped the needle three times before reading, always. Tap tap tap. He had taught Jalen to do the same. The first reading he thought the needle had stuck. The second reading he had sat down on the cold ground in his suit because his knees went odd. Voss's man to his left shifted. "Sir is advised," the man said, without looking at him, "that Helion-Vey Combine filed a flight plan toward your coordinates at 06:00 this morning. For your awareness." Arthur's mouth went dry. Helion-Vey owned Mara's brother's debt. He had bought Jalen's contract from them cheap because Jalen mouthed off. They were not polite like Antares. They sent a boy in an expensive suit and talked about friendship. The *Clarity* shuddered and the spin took them. Through the port, the *Tamerlane* came into view. It was not sleek. It was a riveted can, spinning slowly, patched, with radiator fins that glittered. Terran-built twenty years ago and never updated. Arthur could see the scorch marks near the docks. A voice came over the intercom, tired and female and very clear. "Cutter *Clarity*, you are cleared for hard dock. Passenger Neegan to Conference Three. The High Commissioner is waiting." The harness bit deeper. The ship clanked hard against the station and the vibration stopped all at once, which was worse. One of the dove-grey men undid Arthur's harness. "Seventy-two hours, sir," he said. "That's your charter review window." Arthur stood on legs that didn't want to. He put his hand on the bulkhead to steady himself and left a faint red print. The airlock sighed.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a strong opening chapter that demonstrates genuine craft and a clear understanding of both the Asimov aesthetic and the specific demands of the prompt. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Voice and Style** The prose is deliberately flat and functional in the Asimov tradition, and it largely succeeds. The opening "The transfer vessel Clarity rattled. That was the main thing." is an excellent tonal declaration — it immediately establishes the deflationary register. The narration earns its dryness; it doesn't feel like laziness but like a considered choice. The detail work is strong: "hot bakelite and old sweat," the altimeter needle jumping, the dust in the boot seams. These are specific and tactile without being overwrought. The chapter avoids the "purple tapestry" problem the plan warned against. There are no strained metaphors that don't land. The one moment that approaches poeticism — "The word invite did a strange thing in the room" — is actually quite effective because it's understated and precise. It captures the bureaucratic menace without overexplaining it. **Flashback Structure** The plan called for intercutting a flashback of the armed retinue arriving, and the chapter executes this cleanly. The transition into the flashback is handled without a jarring break — "At 05:30 that morning the dogs had not barked because there were no dogs" is a genuinely good sentence. The absence of dogs as a detail that establishes both the Martian setting and Arthur's isolation is economical and effective. **Character Consistency** Arthur is rendered faithfully to his profile. His first thought when Voss arrives is not resistance — he straightens his shirt. His paternalism shows in the parting words to Jalen and Mara: "Don't touch the geophone" instead of anything human. His hand going to his pocket where the tape is folded is a nice physical tell. The detail about running the tape twice and not wanting to run it a third time is exactly the voice described in the plan: "a third time would make it true." Voss is rendered precisely as planned — literal, blank, professional, the sidearm placed on the table "helpfully." This is the chapter's best moment of dark comedy and it lands without being telegraphed. Mara's "small sound" and Jalen's barefoot silence are consistent with their profiles without being over-explained. **Worldbuilding** The Azra explanation — "Azra made slow atoms fast. That was what the manual said, one sentence." — is exactly right. It's the plain Asimov rule, stated once, without lecture. The Tamerlane described as "a riveted can, spinning slowly, patched, with radiator fins that glittered" and "Terran-built twenty years ago and never updated" is good retrofuturist worldbuilding: lived-in, not curated. The scorch marks near the docks are a nice touch. The Helion-Vey flight plan mention at the end is well-placed — it introduces the third faction without over-explaining, and the detail about Mara's brother's debt is efficiently seeded. **Weaknesses** The chapter is very competent but occasionally safe. The "forty thousand tons" repetition is used three times as a structural beat, which works but is perhaps one time too many. The closing image — Arthur leaving a red handprint on the bulkhead — is the chapter's most overtly "literary" gesture, and it's slightly too neat, a little too symbolic for the register the prose has otherwise established. It's not a disaster, but it's the one moment where the writing reaches for effect rather than earning it. The dialogue is sparse but effective. Voss's lines are excellent — bureaucratic, flat, menacing through procedure. The "For your awareness" repetition is a good character tic. Arthur's dialogue is minimal, which is appropriate for this chapter, though we don't get much sense of his voice yet. The chapter follows its plan closely and faithfully. The beats are all hit: the rattling cutter, the flashback, the inventory violation, the Helion-Vey flight plan, the 72-hour window. The ending on the airlock sigh is appropriately deflationary. **Overall Assessment** This is a well-executed first chapter that successfully establishes tone, character, and stakes without overreaching. It's not a masterpiece — it doesn't take the risks that would make it truly memorable — but it's genuinely good work that serves the prompt and the plan with intelligence and restraint. [Scores] Nuanced Characters: 15 Emotionally Engaging: 14 Compelling Plot: 14 Coherent: 18 Weak Dialogue: 4 Tell-Don't-Show: 4 Unsurprising or Uncreative: 6 Amateurish: 3 Purple Prose: 2 Forced Poetry or Metaphor: 3 Well-earned Lightness or Darkness: 15 Characters Consistent with Profile: 17 Followed Chapter Plan: 18 Faithful to Writing Prompt: 18

**Chapter 2: The Offer** Conference Three was not large. It was wood veneer over aluminum. The veneer was peeling at the corner by the porthole. A radiator hissed too loudly under the porthole and made the room too hot. On the far wall was a ReaDo microfilm reader, the kind with the big green screen and the hand crank. Someone had left a spool in it and the tape was jammed, sticking out at an angle. There were two chairs and a table. The table was bolted to the deck. On it were three things, set square: a mimeographed offer sheet, a thin extract from the Colonial Charter, and an ashtray that was not supposed to be there. High Commissioner Shah stood when he came in and then sat again quickly, as if standing had cost her something. She was small and neat in the same dove-grey as Voss, but her uniform was pressed sharper. Her hair was cut short for suit work, grey at the temples. She had dry hands. She did not look like the voice on the intercom had sounded. She looked tired. "Mr. Neegan," she said. "Thank you for coming. I am Amira Shah." Arthur stood by the door. Voss closed it behind him and took his place by the wall at parade rest. He put his sidearm on the table. He did it the same helpful way he had at the hab. Shah glanced at it, then at Arthur, then away. She flicked a lighter. It didn't light. She flicked it again. Click. Click. She put it down. "Please sit," she said. "You flew up in the hopper. That one rattles. Would you like water?" "No," Arthur said. His voice was too loud in the small room. He sat. The chair was cold. She slid the offer sheet across to him. It was mimeographed, the ink still a little wet and purple. At the top was the seal, the dove and the orbit. Below it, numbers. "This is voluntary," she said. "That matters. Our charter does not allow requisition of a duly held lease. Antares is particular about charters, Mr. Neegan. We are inviting you to transfer mineral rights for Claim 7-B to the Antares Mandate." Arthur looked at the numbers. He had to read them twice. The first number was a lease buyout. It had six zeros after it. The second number was a royalty. The third line said TERRAN CITIZENSHIP - IMMEDIATE - DEPENDENT E. NEEGAN (1). "Citizenship," he said. "For your daughter," Shah said. "And debt clearance for your two indentured. Contract J. Kade and M. Quispe, paid in full, with release papers. Plus the transfer fee, of course. You would be comfortable." She said it plainly, as if she were reading an inventory. Arthur's hand was on the tape in his pocket. He had not taken it out. "My assay," he said. "Forty thousand tons." "Yes," Shah said. "Our survey from orbit said thirty-eight. Yours is better. You have good ground. You were very lucky." "That ground was barren for fourteen years." "Luck is like that," she said. She flicked the dead lighter again. Click. "You understand what Azra is, Mr. Neegan? For our record." He knew the sentence. Everyone knew the sentence. "Azra makes slow atoms fast." "Yes," she said. "A catalyst. You put a little next to uranium and the uranium forgets it was supposed to wait a billion years. It decays now. It gets hot now. That gives us drives. A small pile burns like a star for a week. That also gives us other things. A sub-critical mass becomes critical in a suitcase." She said it without emphasis. She straightened the offer sheet even though it was already straight. "The problem," she said, "is density. One vein like yours lets us build drives for thirty years. Without it, we build for three. The people who don't have it will do things to get it. Helion-Vey filed a flight plan toward your hab at six this morning. They will offer you twice what I am offering and then they will offer something else." Arthur looked at Voss. Voss looked at the wall. "That's the arms race," Shah said. "It is not complicated. Whoever has the heavier pile goes farther and hits harder. Unregulated Azra in private hands is listed as a hazard to navigation. That's the phrase we use." "What does that mean?" Arthur said. "It means we are allowed to be very concerned about private hands," she said. She took her tea. It had three sugars in it. She stirred it ten times, Arthur counted without meaning to, and then didn't drink it. "You have a hab with an expired Model C recycler. That's a hazard, too." There it was. The politeness with the thing underneath. "You said voluntary," Arthur said. "It is," Shah said. "Please read the Charter extract. Article Seven. You will sign that you transfer voluntarily and that you were not coerced. Commander Voss will place his sidearm on the table so you can see we are not coercing you. It's on the table now." Arthur looked down at the Charter extract. The print was small. He knew Article Seven by heart the way a man knows the lease dates. Mineral rights in perpetuity, subject to compliance, transfer must be voluntary and witnessed. He pushed the offer sheet back a half inch. "I get an independent assay and counsel," he said. "Article Seven, paragraph two. Lease-holder may verify and consult." Shah did not seem annoyed. She seemed, if anything, faintly pleased that he had read it. "You do," she said. "Of course you do. We are particular about that." She slid another form toward him. It was white, with red edging. AIR & WATER COMPLIANCE ACKNOWLEDGEMENT - DOME ASSOCIATION 7-B. "Your charter review is in seventy-two hours," she said. "That's the window. You can consult. You can run your own array. We will not interfere. But your hab's permit is expired, Mr. Neegan. Your water allocation is under review. These things take time, and seventy-two hours is not a lot of time to arrange other air." She said it while stirring her tea that she wasn't drinking. Arthur felt the room get hotter. The radiator hissed. Outside the porthole, Mars turned slowly, rust-colored and indifferent. "My crew," he said. "Mara's brother is on Helion-Vey paper." Shah nodded once, as if he had confirmed a note she already had. "Yes. Tharsis. We know. If you transfer to us, that paper is cleared. If you transfer to them, it is not our concern." "And if I transfer to nobody?" Shah finally drank the tea. She made a small face at how sweet it was. "Then you keep a hazard in private hands," she said. "And we remain very concerned. And Helion-Vey will still come. And your recycler will still be out of permit. Seventy-two hours, Mr. Neegan. That is a generous window." She straightened her stack of forms. She clicked the dead lighter one more time and put it away. "You are not a political man, I think," she said. "You are an engineer. Engineers like rules that are literal. I like that, too. The rule says voluntary. So you will volunteer. The question is only to whom." Arthur put his hand flat on the table. His knuckles were dust-ground and his thumbnail was split from tapping the geophone. "I want it in writing," he said. "The seventy-two hours. And the right to assay." "You have it," Shah said. She wrote it on the offer sheet in neat, small handwriting and initialed it. A. SHAH. "We will return you to your hab. Protective observation. For your safety." Voss stepped forward and picked up the sidearm. He holstered it. The movement was precise. Arthur stood. His legs were stiff. "Mr. Neegan," Shah said, not unkindly. "Don't make them come for the second visit. The second visit is not me." She did not stand this time. She was already looking at the next form. At the door, Voss said, "Sir, your dock time is now, sir." They led him back down the riveted corridor. The microfilm reader's jammed tape flapped a little in the draft.

Arthur's responses are appropriately terse and literal — "I want it in writing" — consistent with his engineering mindset. The exchange about Article Seven is particularly well-executed. Arthur finds his footing through the rules, and Shah grants it immediately, which is more frightening than refusal. The compliance form appearing immediately after is a beautiful procedural trap. **Character Consistency** Shah is rendered precisely per her profile: the dead lighter clicked multiple times, the tea stirred exactly ten times (Arthur counts without meaning to — a nice touch), the forms straightened when she's annoyed. Her line "You are not a political man, I think. You are an engineer. Engineers like rules that are literal. I like that, too." is perfectly in character — condescending, accurate, and weaponized as flattery. Arthur's physicality is consistent: the dust-ground knuckles, the split thumbnail from tapping the geophone, the hand flat on the table when cornered. His first instinct to find the loophole (Article Seven, paragraph two) rather than resist emotionally is true to the profile. Voss is appropriately blank and precise. The wood veneer, the hissing radiator, the jammed microfilm reader, the porthole showing Mars, Shah's lighter, the three sugars and ten stirs — all present. The Helion-Vey threat is seeded through the flight plan mention. The compliance form as implicit threat lands cleanly. The plan called for Shah to "hint Helion-Vey will not ask" — this is delivered through "The second visit is not me," which is the chapter's best line. It's menacing without being theatrical. **Weaknesses** The chapter is almost too controlled. There are moments where a little more interiority from Arthur would deepen the emotional engagement — we get his physical responses (legs stiff, room getting hotter) but his internal processing is sparse. The plan's Arthur has a specific relationship to the numbers on that tape; we get "He had to read them twice" but not quite the full weight of what those numbers mean to a man who's been pulling low-grade ilmenite for fourteen years. The line "Luck is like that" from Shah is slightly too aphoristic — it's the one moment where the dialogue edges toward the literary rather than the procedural. The ending with the jammed tape flapping is good but perhaps slightly too neat as a closing image — it risks being the kind of "poetic" button that the plan explicitly wanted to avoid. The chapter is not emotionally devastating in the way the best Asimov can be, but it is consistently intelligent and controlled. The darkness is well-earned through accumulation of procedural detail rather than dramatic gesture. **Overall Assessment** This is a high-quality chapter that successfully executes a difficult tonal challenge. It avoids nearly all the LLM defaults the plan identified. The dialogue is genuinely strong, the bureaucratic menace is real, and the retrofuturist details are integrated rather than decorative. Its weakness is a slight emotional distance that keeps it from being truly memorable rather than merely excellent. A good man can still sell you. I have been sold by good men. Twice." — is the chapter's best moment. It lands flat and stays there, exactly as described. It's the kind of line that earns its darkness because the chapter has built to it honestly. Arthur's complicity is handled with real nuance. The observation rover with the clipboard is a nice touch, but "He had a clipboard" as a sentence fragment feels slightly affected — it's trying for Asimovian dryness but lands closer to stylistic tic. The chapter follows its plan closely: Lyell arrives, makes his threat, Elena argues with Arthur, Arthur reveals his paternalism, he decides to run his own survey. The beats are hit. The plan's instruction to show Arthur's "ugly paternalism" is executed, though the "I kept Jalen and Mara fed when Helion-Vey would have worked them to death" speech is slightly too self-aware as a villain-speech — real paternalists don't usually frame it quite so nakedly. **Overall:** This is a well-executed chapter that delivers on most of its promises. The prose is controlled, the characters are consistent, the darkness is earned, and the dialogue mostly works. **Chapter 8: Equilibrium** Three weeks later the dust had covered the boreholes again. Arthur could see the fence from the hab porthole. It was not a high fence. Just steel posts and wire, strung in a square a kilometer on a side, with a sign every twenty meters that said COLONIAL SCIENCE TRUST - RESTRICTED - NO ENTRY - BY ORDER OF MANDATE. The wire was already going pink with dust. Inside the square was his claim. He could not go in. The hab was the same. The recycler still ran at 112% and still whined. The permit was still expired. Someone from the Dome Association had taped a new notice over the old one on the lock, same red edging, new date: COMPLIANCE REVIEW PENDING - TRUST LITIGATION - 2038. He had eleven years to wait. Mara had made tea. It was reconstituted and weak because they were stretching it. She put a cup by Arthur's hand without saying anything. Her stitches were still blue where the suit was grey. On the galley table were the news slips. Elena had left them before she left. They came off the shortwave on thin paper that curled. Elena had copied the important parts by hand on the back because she didn't trust the tape, same as always. Arthur read them because there was nothing else to read. *— Tamerlane Treaty signed 10/02. Antares Mandate and Helion-Vey Combine agree to joint development moratorium on Azra Plate 7-B pending Earth review. Both parties cite "stability." (Areopolis Review, mimeo, 10/03) —* He turned that slip over. *— Helion-Vey stock down 18% on Azra futures after Trust filing. Analysts cite "devaluation due to poisoning of upper lattice." Company spokesman says borehole flooding was "vandalism." (Tharsis Exchange Bulletin) —* Another. *— Colonial Authority confirms receipt of Form 9-C, Claim 7-B. Legal scholars note precedent: first use of Section 9, Paragraph 4 in 22 years. Case docketed for Earth High Court, 2038. Antares does not contest filing, will "administer site for scientific preservation." Occupation continues. (Dome Association Notice) —* He put that one down. *— Royalties from Trust (if approved) to be applied to buyout of future indenture contracts, prospective only. Association confirms current contracts remain valid and attached to lease-holder for duration. (Addendum, small print, Elena had underlined prospective only twice) —* That was the one Mara had read longest. Jalen came in from outside, helmet under his arm, dust on his shoulders. He was not indentured on paper in the same way now. The Association had reissued his and Mara's papers as Trust Contractors, which meant they earned a wage - a small wage, on paper - and could not be transferred without consent. It also meant they were not freed. The word prospective was literal. Future workers would be bought out, someday, if the court approved, if the royalties ever came. Jalen had 468 days left in his locker count. He had not scratched it out. He had written WAGE next to it in marker. He put a rock on the table. It was smooth, rust-red, worthless. From the plain just outside the fence, where he was allowed to walk. "For the shelf," Jalen said. Arthur picked it up. It was warm from Jalen's glove. He put it on the shelf with the other pebbles, each with a date in faded marker. He had not added a date to this one yet. "They still watching?" Arthur asked. "Rover's gone," Jalen said. "There's a man on the fence now. Dove-grey. He has a clipboard. He counts the wire." Arthur nodded. That sounded like Voss. He went to the geophone box. It was still on the table where he had left it the night of the flooding. The needle was flat, dead against the left stop. No pulse. No tick every 0.82 seconds. Just flatline and the faint hiss of the paper tape feeding blank. He tapped it. Tap tap tap. It didn't move. Mara watched him do it. "Leave it," she said, not unkindly. Elena had left two days after the hearing. She had not shouted. She had been worse than shouting, she had been efficient. She packed her mother's jacket, her notebook of Charter sections, her headset. "You gave it away and you wrecked it in the same night," she had said at the lock, not looking at the fence. "So no one gets it. Not even Mars. You made it worthless to prove you were decent, Dad. That doesn't free anyone. Prospective only. You read that part out loud and then you did it anyway." "It kept Helion-Vey from running crews to death," Arthur said. He had his hands flat on the table, the way he did when he was conserving oxygen. "For this one plate," Elena said. "For eleven years until a court on Earth says the fence is legal. They still have every other plate. You don't even get to keep this one. You're still in a hab with an expired recycler and you still own them." She had glanced at Mara and Jalen then, quick, ashamed to be saying it in front of them. "I'm not—" Arthur started. "You are," Elena said. "You just filed a nicer paper." She hugged Mara. She nodded to Jalen. To Arthur she said, "Cho wants me at the comm station at Marineris. He says we can still use the filing. He says it's a precedent." "Is it?" Arthur asked. Elena had put her hand on the lock. "It's a footnote," she said. And left. The shortwave crackled. Elena's voice sometimes came on it at night, reading League bulletins, but Arthur didn't turn it on much. The hab was quiet except for the recycler. Too quiet, then too loud. Arthur went outside alone before dusk. He didn't bring the array case. He didn't need to. He just walked to the edge of the fence where he was allowed, where the dust was still dust and not Trust property. He had his old slide rule in his pocket and a pebble in his hand that had no date. The plain was flat and rust-colored in every direction. The sun was small. The wind moved a little dust over his boots, into the seams that never came clean. From the fence line he could see Bore Three's cap, white with slurry crust. He had flooded it himself by remote valve while Shah watched the clock tick to midnight. He had made forty-four thousand tons into nothing for the top four hundred meters, where the weapons-grade lattice was. Deeper down it was still there, pure and geometric, but no one could get to it without drilling through his poison and his paperwork at the same time. It would hold. For eleven years, maybe longer. The equilibrium would hold because there was nothing to grab and nothing to file quickly. That was what an engineer called a solution: you didn't fix the load, you removed the load. He turned the pebble over. It was worthless. He had a shelf of them. He liked them because they were his and because they were not worth fighting over. Behind him the hab lights came on. Mara was at the galley table. Jalen was at the gauge. They had stayed. They were wage contractors now who chose to stay, which was different and also not very different, because there was nowhere else to go that paid air. The geophone in the hab would keep feeding blank tape. The radiator would keep hissing. The fence man would keep counting wire with a clipboard. In the Areopolis Review that week there was a small box on page four, under the stock prices, that Elena had not copied. Arthur saw it later when he was using the paper to level the table. *...the Tamerlane equilibrium is expected to hold for the medium term. Analysts note the contribution of the 7-B filing to medium-term stability. The role of the lease-holder was not entered into the official record.* Arthur folded the paper and put it under the table leg where it was needed. Outside, the dust settled.
